intuitionToFormula.ahaInvariant: The triangle grows, but its height ÷ radius stays 0.5 at 30°. The ratio belongs to the angle, not to the size of the triangle.

termMappings.visualPart: The red side, straight up from the ground to P

termMappings.visualPart: The blue side along the ground

sections.heading: 12.1 The longest side
sections.excerpt: The edge across from the square corner. The square corner is the biggest angle in the triangle, and the biggest angle faces the longest side.

steps.text: Pick up a set square. One of its corners is square, like the corner of a page. Which of its three edges is the longest?
The edge across from the square corner. The square corner is the biggest angle in the triangle, and the biggest angle faces the longest side.
Draw a triangle with a square corner, with sides of 3 cm and 4 cm along it. Join their ends and measure the third side. It is 5 cm.
Why must it be the longest? The other two angles add up to 90°, so each is smaller than the square corner. A smaller angle faces a shorter side.
A triangle with one 90° corner is a right-angled triangle. The side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse, and it is always the longest side.
A triangle has sides of 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm, with the right angle between the 6 cm and 8 cm sides. The 10 cm side faces it, so 10 cm is the hypotenuse.
The tempting slip is to call the side at the bottom of the drawing the hypotenuse. Find the right angle first. The hypotenuse is the side that does not touch it.
A right-angled triangle has angles of 90° and 35°. What is its third angle, in degrees?
In a right-angled triangle, the side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse, the longest side.

sections.heading: 12.2 Squares on the sides
sections.excerpt: 4 m. Draw a square on each side of the triangle. The two small squares together cover exactly as much as the big one.

steps.text: A ladder 5 m long leans on a wall, with its foot 3 m out from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
4 m. Draw a square on each side of the triangle. The two small squares together cover exactly as much as the big one.
On squared paper, draw the 3, 4, 5 triangle and a square on each side. Count the small squares: 9 and 16 on the short sides, 25 on the longest.
Why does it always work? Four copies of the triangle fit round a tilted square inside a big square. Move them and the space left over becomes the two smaller squares.
This is Pythagoras' theorem. In a right-angled triangle with shorter sides a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c².
The shorter sides are 5 cm and 12 cm. Then c² = 25 + 144 = 169, and the square root of 169 is 13. So the hypotenuse is 13 cm.
The tempting slip is to add the sides themselves. 3 + 4 = 7, but the hypotenuse of the 3, 4, 5 triangle is 5. Square the sides first.
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is its hypotenuse?
The two shorter sides squared and added make the hypotenuse squared: a² + b² = c².

sections.heading: 12.3 How steep is a ramp
sections.excerpt: Neither. Both rise a quarter of a metre for every metre along, so they make the same angle with the ground.

steps.text: One ramp rises 1 m for every 4 m along the ground. Another rises 2 m for every 8 m. Which is steeper?
Neither. Both rise a quarter of a metre for every metre along, so they make the same angle with the ground.
Draw a ramp 4 cm along and 1 cm up, and another 8 cm along and 2 cm up. Measure the angle at the bottom of each with a protractor.
Why the same angle? The big ramp is an enlargement of the small one with scale factor 2. Its rise and its run double together, so rise ÷ run stays the same.
The angle we are working with is often called θ, said theta. The rise ÷ the run is the tangent of θ, written tan θ. Each angle has its own tangent.
A ramp rises 2 m over 5 m along the ground. tan θ = 2 ÷ 5 = 0.4. Any ramp that rises 0.4 m per metre along makes the same angle θ.
The tempting slip is to divide the run by the rise. The rise goes on top, so a gentle ramp has a small tangent.
A ramp rises 3 m over 4 m along the ground. What is tan θ?
tan θ is the rise ÷ the run. It depends on the angle θ, not on how big the ramp is.

sections.heading: 12.4 Height for every metre of slope
sections.excerpt: Half a metre. At 30°, a ladder reaches up half of its own length, however long the ladder is.

steps.text: A ladder leans at 30° to the ground. How high does it reach for every metre of its length?
Half a metre. At 30°, a ladder reaches up half of its own length, however long the ladder is.
In the figure, set θ to 30° and the radius to 2. The red height is 1. Move the radius up to 4: the height grows to 2, and height ÷ radius stays 0.5.
Why does the ratio stay? Each bigger triangle is an enlargement of the first. Every side is multiplied by the same scale factor, so their ratios do not change.
The height ÷ the slope is the sine of θ, written sin θ. The distance across ÷ the slope is the cosine of θ, written cos θ. So sin 30° = 0.5.
A ladder 6 m long makes 30° with the ground. Its top is 6 × sin 30° = 6 × 0.5 = 3 m up the wall.
The tempting slip is to divide by the side along the ground. Sine and cosine divide by the slope, the hypotenuse. Only tangent divides by the run.
A ramp 8 m long makes 30° with the ground, and sin 30° = 0.5. How high does it rise?
sin θ is height ÷ hypotenuse and cos θ is across ÷ hypotenuse. Both belong to the angle, whatever the size.

sections.heading: 12.5 One circle for every angle
sections.excerpt: Your spoke is the hypotenuse, 1 unit long. So your height is sin θ and your distance across is cos θ.

steps.text: You sit on a Ferris wheel whose spokes are 1 unit long. As it turns, how high above the hub and how far to the side are you?
Your spoke is the hypotenuse, 1 unit long. So your height is sin θ and your distance across is cos θ.
Draw a circle of radius 10 cm centred on (0, 0). Mark the point at 30° round from the right. Measure its height, 5 cm, and its distance across, about 8.7 cm.
Why do the squares add up to 1? The height, the distance across and the spoke make a right-angled triangle. Pythagoras' theorem says height² + across² = 1².
A circle of radius 1 centred on (0, 0) is the unit circle. The point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ). The rule sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is the Pythagorean identity.
At 30°, sin θ = 0.5, so sin²θ = 0.25. Then cos²θ = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, and cos 30° is about 0.866.
The tempting slip is to think sin θ + cos θ = 1. At 30° that would make cos 30° = 0.5. It is the squares that add to 1.
For an angle less than 90°, sin θ = 0.6. Use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to find cos θ.
On the unit circle the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ), and sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 at every angle.

sections.heading: 12.6 Measuring a turn by its arc
sections.excerpt: A little less than 60°, about 57°. The angle depends only on how many radii fit along the arc, not on the size of the circle.

steps.text: Cut a piece of string as long as a circle's radius, and lay it round the edge of the circle. What angle does it make at the centre?
A little less than 60°, about 57°. The angle depends only on how many radii fit along the arc, not on the size of the circle.
Draw a circle of radius 5 cm and bend a 5 cm strip of paper along its edge. Join both ends of the strip to the centre and measure the angle.
Why about 57°? The whole circumference is 2π radii long, about 6.28 of them. So one radius of arc is 360° ÷ 6.28, about 57.3°.
An angle whose arc is one radius long is 1 radian. A full turn is 2π radians and a half turn is π radians.
A half turn is 180°, which is π radians, about 3.14. So 90°, half of that, is π ÷ 2 radians, about 1.57.
The tempting slip is to read 1 radian as 1°. A radian is far bigger: about 57 degrees fit inside it.
A full turn is 2π radians, about 6.28. How many radians is a quarter turn, to 2 decimal places?
One radian is the angle whose arc is one radius long. A full turn is 2π radians.

sections.heading: 12.7 Triangles with no right angle
sections.excerpt: Yes. Drop a line from one corner straight down to the opposite side. That splits the field into two right-angled triangles that share their height.

steps.text: A field is a triangle with no square corner. Can you still find a side you cannot reach from a side and two angles you can measure?
Yes. Drop a line from one corner straight down to the opposite side. That splits the field into two right-angled triangles that share their height.
Draw any triangle ABC and drop a line from C straight down to AB. Label the side across from A as a, and the side across from B as b.
Why do the two sides match up? The shared height is b × sin A in one triangle and a × sin B in the other. So b × sin A = a × sin B.
Divide both sides and you get the sine rule: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. Each side ÷ the sine of the angle across from it gives the same number.
In a triangle, a = 6 cm, sin A = 0.5 and sin B = 0.8. Then b = 6 × 0.8 ÷ 0.5 = 9.6 cm.
The tempting slip is to pair a side with an angle at one of its own ends. Each side goes with the angle across from it.
In a triangle, a = 8 cm, sin A = 0.4 and sin B = 0.6. Use the sine rule to find b.
In any triangle, each side ÷ the sine of the angle across from it gives the same number.

sections.heading: 12.8 Pythagoras with a correction
sections.excerpt: 7 cm. With a right angle it would be about 9.4 cm, from Pythagoras' theorem. A smaller angle pulls the ends closer, so you take something away.

steps.text: Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 8 cm, with 60° between them. How long is the third side?
7 cm. With a right angle it would be about 9.4 cm, from Pythagoras' theorem. A smaller angle pulls the ends closer, so you take something away.
Hinge two sticks of 5 cm and 8 cm together. Open them to 90°, then close them to 60°. Watch the gap between their free ends shrink.
Why take away 2ab cos C? Cosine measures how much one side leans along the other. At 90° the lean is zero and the rule turns back into Pythagoras' theorem.
The cosine rule says c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, where C is the angle between sides a and b.
Sides of 3 cm and 5 cm meet at 60°, and cos 60° = 0.5. Then c² = 9 + 25 − 2 × 3 × 5 × 0.5 = 19, so c is about 4.36 cm.
The tempting slip is to use an angle that is not between the two known sides. The angle C must sit where sides a and b meet.
Sides of 5 cm and 8 cm meet at 60°, and cos 60° = 0.5. Use the cosine rule to find the third side.
The cosine rule c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C is Pythagoras' theorem with a correction for the angle.

debate.title: Double the angle, double the sine?
debate.contextPrompt: sin 30° = 0.5. Asha and Rohan argue about sin 60°.
debate.speakerAClaim: 60° is twice 30°, so sin 60° is twice 0.5. That makes it 1.
debate.speakerBClaim: sin 60° can't be 1. That would make the height as long as the slope, and only 90° does that.

choices.reasoningStatement: The angle doubles, so the height for every metre of slope doubles too.
choices.socraticRebuttal: If sin 60° were 1, the height would equal the slope. What would sin 90° be, and could any height be longer than the slope?

choices.speakerLabel: Rohan is right (sin 60° is less than 1)
choices.reasoningStatement: The height can never be longer than the slope, and only a 90° angle makes them equal.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. sin 60° is about 0.866. Doubling an angle does not double its sine: the height grows more and more slowly near 90°.

choices.speakerLabel: Neither. It depends how big the triangle is.
choices.reasoningStatement: A bigger triangle has a bigger height.
choices.socraticRebuttal: A bigger triangle has a longer slope too. What happens to height ÷ slope when both grow by the same scale factor?

debate.invariantTakeaway: A sine belongs to its angle, but it does not grow in step with it: sin 60° is about 0.866, not twice sin 30°.

skillCard.skill: Designing a fair sample by random, systematic or stratified choice, and spotting when a survey leaves an important group out

sheCan.prompt: With no calculator: a school has 240 Year 7 students, 180 Year 8 students and 180 Year 9 students, 600 in all. How many from each year belong in a fair sample of 50? And if you pick 20 names at even steps from a list of 600, what step size do you use?
sheCan.answer: Year 7 is 240 ÷ 600 × 50 = 20, Year 8 is 180 ÷ 600 × 50 = 15, and Year 9 is 15. For 20 names from 600, step through every 600 ÷ 20 = 30th name.

skillCard.whyItMatters: Doctors testing a medicine, pollsters before an election and engineers checking factory parts can never test everyone. A fair sample tells the truth about the whole group; a lopsided one fools you even when it is huge.

sections.heading: 13.1 Tasting the soup without drinking the pot
sections.excerpt: She stirs the pot well and tastes one spoonful. When the pot is well mixed, a small spoonful tells the truth about the whole pot.

steps.text: A cook makes a 10-litre pot of dal. How does she know if it needs more salt without eating the whole pot?
She stirs the pot well and tastes one spoonful. When the pot is well mixed, a small spoonful tells the truth about the whole pot.
Picture 600 folded slips of paper in a drum, one for each student in a school. Shake the drum and pull out 30 slips with your eyes shut.
Why shut your eyes and shake the drum? If you only ask your own table at lunch, you get your friends' habits, not the school's. Giving every person the same chance keeps favourites out.
The whole group you want to know about is the population. A smaller group chosen from it is a sample. When every member of the population has the same chance of being chosen, it is a random sample.
A school has 600 students. Number them 1 to 600 and let a computer pick 30 numbers with equal chance. The 600 students are the population, and the 30 chosen are a random sample.
The tempting slip is to think 'random' means picking whoever walks past first. That leaves out everyone in a classroom or on another floor. Use numbered slips or a random number list.
A factory bakes 2,000 biscuits and picks 40 of them by lot to test their weight. How many biscuits are in the population?
The population is the whole group, a sample is the part you test, and a random sample gives everyone the same chance.

sections.heading: 13.2 Stepping through a list and matching group shares
sections.excerpt: No. Year 7 is twice as big as Year 8, so it should get twice as many places in the sample: 20 from Year 7 and 10 from Year 8.

steps.text: A school has 400 students in Year 7 and 200 in Year 8. If you want 30 students in your sample, should you pick 15 from each year?
No. Year 7 is twice as big as Year 8, so it should get twice as many places in the sample: 20 from Year 7 and 10 from Year 8.
Draw a bar of 6 equal blocks for the 600 students: 4 blocks for Year 7 and 2 blocks for Year 8. Share the 30 sample places across the 6 blocks: 5 in each block.

Why not 15 and 15? Taking 15 from each gives Year 8 half the voice in the sample when they are only a third of the school. Matching each group's fraction keeps the sample in the same ratio as the school.

When you split the population into groups and pick from each group in proportion to its size, you take a stratified sample. When you line everyone up on a numbered list and pick every kth person from a random start, you take a systematic sample.
To pick a systematic sample of 20 from a list of 600 names, divide 600 ÷ 20 = 30. Pick a random start between 1 and 30, say 7, then take the 7th, 37th, 67th, and every 30th name.
The tempting slip in a stratified sample is to divide the sample equally among the groups. Always multiply the sample size by group size ÷ total population.
A club has 120 juniors and 80 seniors, 200 members in all. In a stratified sample of 40 members, how many juniors should be chosen?
A systematic sample takes every kth item on a list; a stratified sample gives each group its true fraction of the sample.

sections.heading: 13.3 The planes that did not come back
sections.excerpt: Because people who never go to a gym had zero chance of being asked. Your method favoured early-morning gym-goers before a single question was answered.

steps.text: Wanting to know how many hours people in Mumbai exercise, you ask 100 people leaving a gym at 6 am. Why will your answer be too high?
Because people who never go to a gym had zero chance of being asked. Your method favoured early-morning gym-goers before a single question was answered.
Picture the outline of a Second World War plane. Returning planes are covered in bullet holes along the wings and tail, while the engine boxes are clean.

Why did the mathematician Abraham Wald put armour on the clean engines instead of the riddled wings? Enemy bullets hit every part equally. Planes hit in the wings flew home to be counted; planes hit in the engine crashed and were missing from the shed.

When a sampling method favours some parts of the population over others, the sample has bias. When you only see the ones that survived a test or a journey and forget the ones that dropped out, that is survivorship bias.
Reading only five-star reviews from customers who kept a phone for two years misses everyone who returned it in the first week. That is survivorship bias.
The tempting slip is to think a bigger sample cures bias. Asking 10,000 people outside the gym still misses everyone asleep at home. Fix how you pick, not how many.
Out of 50 planes sent out, 8 are hit in the engine and all 8 crash. The other 42 return with wing hits. How many engine-hit planes are in the shed to be counted?
Bias happens when some members are more likely to be picked than others; survivorship bias happens when dropouts are invisible.

sections.heading: 13.4 Why four times the sample halves the wobble
sections.excerpt: Rohan's. This step goes beyond the school book. Because 64 is 4 times 16, and the square root of 4 is 2, Rohan's typical error is half as wide as Asha's.

steps.text: Two students each estimate the average height in their school using a fair random sample. Asha measures 16 students; Rohan measures 64. Whose estimate is likely to sit closer to the true school figure?
Rohan's. This step goes beyond the school book. Because 64 is 4 times 16, and the square root of 4 is 2, Rohan's typical error is half as wide as Asha's.
In the figure, keep the population spread at 12 and move the sample size from 16 to 64. Watch the red bracket shrink from 3 down to 1.5.
Why does the error divide by √n instead of n? In a random group, high values and low values partly cancel each other out. The leftover wobble shrinks with the square root of the group size.
Adding the values and dividing by how many there are gives the mean. The typical gap between a sample mean and the population mean is the standard error, σ ÷ √n.
If the population spread σ is 12 cm and you take a sample of n = 16 students, the standard error is 12 ÷ √16 = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm. With n = 64 students, it drops to 12 ÷ √64 = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 cm.
The tempting slip is to think doubling the sample size halves the standard error. Because of the square root, you must multiply the sample size by 4 to halve the standard error.
A population has spread σ = 20, and you take a random sample of n = 25 items. Using σ ÷ √n, what is the standard error?
The standard error is σ ÷ √n, so multiplying a random sample's size by 4 cuts the typical error of the mean in half.

callouts.body: Explain to a friend why Abraham Wald told the engineers to armour the parts of the returning planes that had no bullet holes.

debate.title: Equal numbers or equal shares?
debate.contextPrompt: A school has 300 students in Year 7 and 100 in Year 8. Asha and Rohan want a stratified sample of 40 students.
debate.speakerAClaim: There are two year groups, so a fair sample takes the same number from each: 20 from Year 7 and 20 from Year 8.
debate.speakerBClaim: Year 7 is three quarters of the school, so it gets three quarters of the sample: 30 from Year 7 and 10 from Year 8.

choices.reasoningStatement: Every group should have the same number of people in the sample.
choices.socraticRebuttal: If Year 8 gets 20 out of 40 places, it has half the sample even though it is only a quarter of the school.

choices.reasoningStatement: Each group gets the same fraction of the sample as its fraction of the whole school.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. 300 ÷ 400 × 40 = 30 from Year 7 and 100 ÷ 400 × 40 = 10 from Year 8, so every student has the same 1 in 10 chance.

choices.speakerLabel: Neither. Take all 40 from Year 7 because it is the largest group.
choices.reasoningStatement: Only the biggest group matters for the school average.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Leaving Year 8 out completely gives a biased sample with zero voice for a quarter of the school.

debate.invariantTakeaway: In a stratified sample, each group's share of the sample matches its share of the whole population.

chapters.title: Spread: histograms and standard deviation
chapters.subtitle: School book chapter 10 · Smoothing a bumpy line over time, ordering leaves, drawing bars whose area is the count, and measuring spread
chapters.hookSummary: Two bus routes both take 20 minutes on average. One arrives in 19, 20 or 21 minutes; the other takes 5 minutes or 35. The average alone hides the wait.

skillCard.skill: Reading and drawing time-series graphs, stem-and-leaf diagrams and unequal-width histograms, and comparing two sets of data by their middle and their spread

sheCan.prompt: With no calculator: in a survey of parcel masses, the group 40 ≤ m < 60 kg holds 30 parcels and the group 60 ≤ m < 70 kg holds 25 parcels. What height should each bar have on a histogram? And for the seven numbers 12, 15, 17, 20, 24, 29, 31, what are the middle value and the spread of the middle half?
sheCan.answer: For 40 to 60 kg the width is 20, so the bar height is 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5. For 60 to 70 kg the width is 10, so the bar height is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5. For the seven numbers, the middle value is 20, and the middle half runs from 15 to 29, a spread of 29 − 15 = 14.

skillCard.whyItMatters: Averages without spread can mislead a hospital, a weather office or a shopper. Knowing how wide the bars are and how far values sit from the middle lets you read the whole shape of the data.

sections.heading: 14.1 Smoothing out the bumps across time
sections.excerpt: Plot the days in order along the bottom, then take the mean of each run of 7 days. Every 7-day window holds one Saturday and one Monday, so the weekly bumps flatten out.

steps.text: An ice-cream stall writes down its sales every day for a month. Weekends spike high and Mondays dip low. How can the owner see whether the month as a whole is climbing?
Plot the days in order along the bottom, then take the mean of each run of 7 days. Every 7-day window holds one Saturday and one Monday, so the weekly bumps flatten out.
Picture a jagged mountain path of daily dots, and a smooth ribbon running through the middle of every three consecutive dots.
Why slide the window one step at a time? Each step drops the oldest day and adds the newest day. One hot Saturday cannot pull the whole ribbon up on its own.
A graph with time along the horizontal axis and readings plotted in order is a time series. The mean of a sliding window of fixed length, such as 3 days or 4 quarters, is a moving average.
Daily sales over four days are 10, 14, 18 and 22. The first 3-day moving average is (10 + 14 + 18) ÷ 3 = 14, and the next is (14 + 18 + 22) ÷ 3 = 18.
The tempting slip is to plot a moving average above the last day of its window. Plot it above the middle of its window so the trend line is not shifted sideways.
Rainfall over three months is 12 mm, 18 mm and 24 mm. What is their 3-month moving average, in mm?
A time series plots readings in time order, and a moving average smooths regular ups and downs to show the underlying trend.

sections.heading: 14.2 Keeping every digit while showing the shape
sections.excerpt: The middle number when they are lined up in order, 20. And to measure the spread without being fooled by the 95-minute puncture, take the gap across the middle half of the riders: 29 − 15 = 14.

steps.text: Seven cyclists finish a hill climb in 12, 15, 17, 20, 24, 29 and 31 minutes. If one cyclist had a puncture and took 95 minutes instead of 31, the mean jumps up. What measure of the middle stays at 20?
The middle number when they are lined up in order, 20. And to measure the spread without being fooled by the 95-minute puncture, take the gap across the middle half of the riders: 29 − 15 = 14.
Write the tens digit on the left of a line and the ordered units digits on the right: 1 | 2 5 7, 2 | 0 4 9, 3 | 1. Add the key: 1 | 2 means 12 minutes.
Why cut off the bottom quarter and the top quarter? Extreme outliers live at the two ends. The middle half shows how spread out typical riders are.

Splitting each number into a tens stem and an ordered units leaf makes a stem-and-leaf diagram. In an ordered list, the middle value is the median. The middles of the two halves are the quartiles Q₁ and Q₃, and Q₃ − Q₁ is the interquartile range.

For 12, 15, 17, 20, 24, 29, 31, the 4th value is the median, 20. The lower three values 12, 15, 17 have middle Q₁ = 15; the upper three 24, 29, 31 have middle Q₃ = 29; so the interquartile range is 29 − 15 = 14.
The tempting slip in a stem-and-leaf diagram is to leave the leaves unsorted or forget the key. Without ascending leaves you cannot count to the median, and without a key 2 | 4 could mean 24 or 2.4.
Find the interquartile range of the seven ordered numbers 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28.
A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every exact value in order; the median marks the middle and the interquartile range Q₃ − Q₁ measures the middle half.

sections.heading: 14.3 Why area, not height, is the count
sections.excerpt: Because the group from 20 to 45 minutes is 25 minutes wide, two and a half times as wide as the 10-minute groups. Making it 30 units tall as well makes its rectangle look huge, even though only 1.2 patients arrived per minute.

steps.text: Waiting times at a clinic are grouped into 0 to 10 minutes (18 patients), 10 to 20 minutes (24 patients), and one wide group from 20 to 45 minutes (30 patients). If you draw a bar of height 30 for the wide group, why does the chart lie?

Because the group from 20 to 45 minutes is 25 minutes wide, two and a half times as wide as the 10-minute groups. Making it 30 units tall as well makes its rectangle look huge, even though only 1.2 patients arrived per minute.
In the figure, look at the three bars when the third group's width is 25 minutes and its count is 30. Its height is 30 ÷ 25 = 1.2, so the area of the red rectangle is 25 × 1.2 = 30.
Why divide the count by the width? The eye judges a bar by the ink it covers, which is its area. Setting height = count ÷ width guarantees that area = width × height = count.

The span of a group from its lower edge to its upper edge is the class width. The count divided by the class width is the frequency density. A chart of continuous groups with no gaps where bar height is frequency density and bar area is the count is a histogram.

For 40 ≤ m < 60 kg with 30 parcels, the class width is 60 − 40 = 20 kg and the frequency density is 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5. For 60 ≤ m < 70 kg with 25 parcels, the class width is 10 kg and the frequency density is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5.

The tempting slip is to plot the raw count on the vertical axis when the groups have unequal widths. Always divide count by class width first, and multiply frequency density by class width to read a count back.
A group 10 ≤ t < 25 seconds has class width 15 seconds and frequency density 3.2. How many items are in this group?
In a histogram, frequency density is count ÷ class width, so the area of every bar equals the count in that group.

sections.heading: 14.4 Distance from the balance point
sections.excerpt: Square each gap before adding, take the mean of those squares, then take the square root to return to the starting units. This calculation goes beyond the school book, which only asks you to compare spreads.

steps.text: Five friends score 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 on a quiz. Their mean is 8. If you find each score's gap from 8 (−4, −2, 0, +2, +4) and add those gaps up, you get 0. How do we stop the negative gaps cancelling the positive ones?

Square each gap before adding, take the mean of those squares, then take the square root to return to the starting units. This calculation goes beyond the school book, which only asks you to compare spreads.
Picture a plank balanced on a pivot at 8, with blocks at 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Each block's distance from the pivot is squared: 16, 4, 0, 4 and 16.

Why take the square root at the end? Squaring turns marks into squared marks, or metres into square metres. Taking the square root brings the spread back into marks or metres so you can compare it with the mean.

The Greek capital letter Σ, called sigma, means 'add up all the terms of this kind'. The mean of the squared gaps from the mean, Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n, is the variance. Its square root is the standard deviation, written σ.
For 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, the mean is 8 and the squared gaps are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16. Their sum Σ(x − 8)² is 40, the variance is 40 ÷ 5 = 8, and the standard deviation is σ = √8 ≈ 2.83.
The tempting slip is to stop at the variance, 8, and forget the square root. A spread of 8 marks would be wider than the gap from 8 to the highest score, 12. Take the square root to get √8 ≈ 2.83.
Four numbers 2, 4, 6 and 8 have a mean of 5. Their gaps from 5 are −3, −1, 1 and 3, so the squared gaps are 9, 1, 1 and 9. What is their variance, Σ(x − 5)² ÷ 4?
Variance averages the squared distances from the mean using Σ, and standard deviation σ takes the square root to measure typical spread.

debate.title: Does the tallest bar hold the most people?
debate.contextPrompt: On a journey-time histogram, group A (width 10 minutes) has frequency density 4, and group B (width 30 minutes) has frequency density 2.
debate.speakerAClaim: Group A's bar is twice as tall as group B's (4 against 2), so twice as many people are in group A.
debate.speakerBClaim: In a histogram, the area is the count. Group A holds 10 × 4 = 40 people, while group B holds 30 × 2 = 60 people.

choices.speakerLabel: Asha is right (group A has more)
choices.reasoningStatement: The tallest bar always shows the biggest count.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Height matches the count only when every bar has the same width. Here group B is three times as wide as group A.

choices.speakerLabel: Rohan is right (group B has 60, group A has 40)
choices.reasoningStatement: Count equals frequency density × class width, which is the area of the bar.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Group A is more crowded per minute, but group B spans 30 minutes and holds 30 × 2 = 60 people in total.

choices.speakerLabel: Neither. They hold the same number of people.
choices.reasoningStatement: A wider bar and a taller bar cancel each other out.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Multiply width by height for each bar: 10 × 4 = 40, while 30 × 2 = 60.

debate.invariantTakeaway: In a histogram, the area of a bar (class width × frequency density) equals the count in that group.

A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles, and two are drawn without putting the first back. What is the chance both are red? And how many 3-person teams can be chosen from 8 students?

skillCard.whyItMatters: Games, weather forecasts, genetics and quality checks all rest on counting how many ways something can happen out of all equally likely ways.

sections.heading: 15.1 Why 7 beats 12 six to one
sections.excerpt: No. A total of 12 happens in only one way, 6 on red and 6 on blue. A total of 7 happens in six ways: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1).

steps.text: You roll a red die and a blue die and add them. There are 11 possible totals, from 2 to 12. Does each total have a 1 in 11 chance?
No. A total of 12 happens in only one way, 6 on red and 6 on blue. A total of 7 happens in six ways: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2) and (6,1).
Draw a 6 × 6 grid with red 1 to 6 along the side and blue 1 to 6 along the top. Count the 36 squares, and shade the diagonal of four squares that add to 9: (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3).
Why count the 36 pairs instead of the 11 totals? Each of the 36 pairs is equally likely, 1 in 36. The 11 totals are not equally likely because different numbers of pairs make them.

One possible result of a trial is an outcome, and the complete list or grid of all possible results is the sample space. When outcomes are equally likely, the probability of a result is wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes, on a scale from 0 to 1. Results that cannot happen at the same time are mutually exclusive; their probabilities add up, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
On the 36-square grid for two fair dice, four squares add to 9. So the probability of a sum of 9 is 4 ÷ 36 = 1/9, and the probability of not getting 9 is 1 − 1/9 = 8/9.
The tempting slip is to treat (3, 6) and (6, 3) as one outcome. Red 3 with blue 6 and red 6 with blue 3 are two separate squares on the 36-square grid.
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that their sum is 11, as a fraction in simplest form?
List the sample space of equally likely outcomes first; probability is wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

sections.heading: 15.2 Testing a coin and multiplying along a tree
sections.excerpt: Because only 7 marbles are left in the bag. If the first marble was red, only 4 of the remaining 7 are red, so the chance of two reds is 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

steps.text: A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles, 8 in all. You pick one marble, keep it out, and pick a second. Why does the fraction for the second marble change?
Because only 7 marbles are left in the bag. If the first marble was red, only 4 of the remaining 7 are red, so the chance of two reds is 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.
Draw two branches from the start labeled Red (5/8) and Blue (3/8). From the Red tip, split into Red (4/7) and Blue (3/7), and multiply along the top path: 5/8 × 4/7.
Why multiply along the branches? Five eighths of the time you take the top branch, and four sevenths of those times you take the next top branch. Four sevenths of five eighths is 5/8 × 4/7.

A probability estimated from real trials, count of successes ÷ number of trials, is an experimental probability. Two stages where the first result does not change the chances of the second are independent events, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). A branching picture that writes each step's fractions on its branches is a tree diagram.
If you put the first marble back before picking the second, the two picks are independent events: P(both red) = 5/8 × 5/8 = 25/64. Without replacement they are not: P(both red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 5/14.
The tempting slip is to add along a path, writing 5/8 + 4/7. Multiply along the branches to follow one path; add at the end only when combining two separate paths.
A bag holds 4 green and 2 yellow counters, 6 in all. Two counters are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are green, in simplest form?
On a tree diagram, multiply along branches for one path and add separate paths. Only independent events keep the same fractions on the second step.

sections.heading: 15.3 When order matters and when it does not
sections.excerpt: For medals, there are 8 choices for Gold, 7 for Silver and 6 for Bronze: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 ways. For a team, the same 3 students can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 medal orders, so divide 336 by 6 to get 56 teams.

steps.text: From 8 students, how many ways can you award Gold, Silver and Bronze medals? How does that count change for an equal 3-person team?

For medals, there are 8 choices for Gold, 7 for Silver and 6 for Bronze: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336 ways. For a team, the same 3 students can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 medal orders, so divide 336 by 6 to get 56 teams.
Draw three medal boxes [8][7][6]. Underneath, group the 6 rearrangements of Asha, Rohan and Meera into one single team box.
Why divide by 6? In a team there is no Gold, Silver or Bronze. Every group of 3 people was counted 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 times in the ordered list, so dividing by 6 counts each team once.

This section goes beyond the school book. The product of all whole numbers from n down to 1 is n factorial, written n!. An ordered arrangement of r items from n is a permutation, ⁿPᵣ = n! ÷ (n − r)!. An unordered selection of r items from n is a combination, ⁿCᵣ = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!).
4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. To choose 2 captains of equal rank from 6 players, calculate ⁶C₂ = (6 × 5) ÷ (2 × 1) = 15 pairs.
The tempting slip is to use ⁿPᵣ when order does not matter. Ask whether swapping two picked people changes the result: if not, divide by r! to get a combination.
How many different 2-topping pizzas can you choose from 7 toppings, where the order of the two toppings does not matter?
n! multiplies from n down to 1; a permutation counts ordered picks, and a combination divides by r! when order does not matter.

sections.heading: 15.4 Dropping balls through a pegboard
sections.excerpt: Because there is only 1 path that goes right all 6 times, but there are ⁶C₃ = 20 different paths that go right 3 times and left 3 times.

steps.text: A ball drops through 6 rows of pegs, bouncing left or right with a 50% chance at each peg. Why do most balls pile up in the middle slots instead of spreading evenly across the bottom?
Because there is only 1 path that goes right all 6 times, but there are ⁶C₃ = 20 different paths that go right 3 times and left 3 times.
In the figure, set the pegboard rows to 6, the slot to 3, and the bounce chance to 50%. Read the path counts above the bars: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1, adding up to 64 paths in all.
Why is the count in slot k equal to ⁿCₖ? Choosing a path to slot k means choosing which k of the n rows bounce right. That is a combination of k rows out of n.
As the number of rows grows, the tall middle bars and low outer tails smooth into the symmetric shape called a bell curve.
With 6 rows at 50%, there are 2⁶ = 64 equally likely paths. Slot 3 has ⁶C₃ = 20 paths, so the probability of landing in slot 3 is 20 ÷ 64 = 5/16 = 31.25%.
The tempting slip is to think a ball 'aims' for the middle. Every single path has the same 1 in 64 chance; the middle wins only because 20 paths lead there.
A ball drops through 4 rows of pegs (n = 4). How many paths ⁴C₂ land in the middle slot (k = 2)?
Slot k after n rows of pegs collects ⁿCₖ paths, piling most balls in the middle to form a bell curve.

debate.title: One head and one tail: two outcomes or three?
debate.contextPrompt: Two fair coins, a ₹1 coin and a ₹2 coin, are tossed together. Asha and Rohan argue about the probability of getting one Head and one Tail.
debate.speakerAClaim: There are three possible results: two Heads, two Tails, or one of each. So one Head and one Tail has probability 1/3.
debate.speakerBClaim: The 2 × 2 sample space has four equally likely outcomes: HH, HT, TH and TT. Both HT and TH give one of each, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2.

choices.reasoningStatement: HT and TH are the same result, so there are only 3 outcomes.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Head on the ₹1 coin with Tail on the ₹2 coin is a different physical outcome from Tail on ₹1 with Head on ₹2.

choices.reasoningStatement: Of the 4 equally likely pairs in the sample space, 2 pairs (HT and TH) have one Head and one Tail.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Listing all 4 equally likely pairs in the sample space shows that HT and TH together take up 2 out of 4 squares.

choices.reasoningStatement: Multiply 1/2 for Head by 1/2 for Tail.
choices.socraticRebuttal: 1/4 is the probability of HT alone. Adding TH (another 1/4) gives 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

debate.invariantTakeaway: Count equally likely pairs in the full sample space: HT and TH are two separate ways to get one Head and one Tail.

chapters.subtitle: Beyond the school book · Why a 95% accurate test on a rare condition is right only 28% of the time, worked out in 1,000 people before any formula
chapters.hookSummary: A medical test is 95% accurate, and you test positive for a condition that affects 2 in 100 people. Why is the chance you actually have it only about 28%, not 95%?

skillCard.skill: Turning percentages into counts out of 1,000 people to update a probability when new evidence arrives

sheCan.prompt: With no calculator: out of 1,000 people, 2% (20 people) have a trait and 980 do not. A test flags 95% of the 20 who have it, and also falsely flags 5% of the 980 who do not. How many people test positive in all, and what fraction of them actually have the trait?
sheCan.answer: 95% of 20 is 19 true positives, and 5% of 980 is 49 false positives. In all, 19 + 49 = 68 people test positive, and 19/68 (about 27.9%) actually have the trait.

skillCard.whyItMatters: Doctors reading a scan, spam filters checking an email and detectives weighing a clue all update a starting chance when new evidence arrives.

intuitionToFormula.concreteAction: In the figure, set the condition rate to 2%, the true-hit rate to 95%, and the false-alarm rate to 5%.
intuitionToFormula.ahaInvariant: Out of 1,000 people, everyone who tested negative disappears. Only two bars remain: 19 sick people flagged red and 49 healthy people flagged amber, so 19 out of 68 are sick.
intuitionToFormula.formulaDisplay: P(sick | +) = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives)

termMappings.visualPart: The amber rectangle on the right (49 of 1,000)

sections.heading: 16.1 Narrowing the world when you learn a clue
sections.excerpt: Before you see the helmet, the chance is 20 out of 1,000, or 2%. Once you see the helmet, you stop dividing by all 1,000 students and divide only by the students carrying a helmet.

steps.text: In a school of 1,000 students, 20 cycle to school and 980 walk or take the bus. What is the chance a student cycles before you look, and how does it change if they hold a cycle helmet?
Before you see the helmet, the chance is 20 out of 1,000, or 2%. Once you see the helmet, you stop dividing by all 1,000 students and divide only by the students carrying a helmet.
Draw a box of 1,000 dots, with a narrow strip of 20 cyclists on the left and 980 non-cyclists on the right. Draw a circle around only the dots holding a helmet; that circle is your new denominator.
Why does the denominator shrink? Everyone without a helmet is ruled out by what you saw. Probabilities must be counted inside the group that matches the clue.

The starting share of a group in the whole population, such as 20 in 1,000 (2%), is the base rate. Your starting probability before seeing the clue is the prior. The probability of A given that B has happened is the conditional probability, written P(A | B), read 'the probability of A given B'.
In a two-way table, 30 students play chess, and 12 of those 30 also play tabla. Given that a student plays chess, the conditional probability they play tabla is 12 ÷ 30 = 2/5.
The tempting slip is to keep dividing by the whole 1,000 after you know the clue happened. The vertical bar in P(A | B) means 'restrict the denominator to B'.
In a club of 100 members, 25 wear glasses, and 10 of those 25 are left-handed. Given that a member wears glasses, what is the conditional probability they are left-handed, in simplest form?
The base rate gives your prior before the clue; conditional probability P(A | B) shrinks the denominator to only the cases where B happened.

sections.heading: 16.2 Two ways a test can be right, and how false alarms pile up
sections.excerpt: 5% of 980, which is 49 healthy people. Even a small 5% slip rate makes a big pile of 49 wrong alarms when it acts on a crowd of 980 healthy people.

steps.text: Out of 1,000 people, 20 are sick and 980 are healthy. A test catches 95% of the 20 sick people, and it is 95% accurate on the 980 healthy people too. How many healthy people still get a wrong positive result?
5% of 980, which is 49 healthy people. Even a small 5% slip rate makes a big pile of 49 wrong alarms when it acts on a crowd of 980 healthy people.
Split a bar of 1,000 people into 20 sick on the left and 980 healthy on the right. Colour 19 of the 20 red (0.95 × 20 = 19), and colour 49 of the 980 amber (0.05 × 980 = 49).
Why are there more amber boxes (49) than red boxes (19)? Because healthy people outnumber sick people 980 to 20. Five per cent of a huge crowd beats ninety-five per cent of a tiny group.

The share of sick people the test rightly flags positive is its sensitivity (here 19 out of 20, or 95%). The share of healthy people the test rightly clears negative is its specificity (here 931 out of 980, or 95%). A healthy person wrongly flagged positive is a false positive (here the remaining 5% of 980, which is 49 people).
If 500 people are healthy and a test has 98% specificity, then 98% of 500 = 490 test negative, and the remaining 2% of 500 = 10 are false positives.
The tempting slip is to take 5% of all 1,000 people instead of 5% of the 980 healthy people. Sensitivity acts on the sick group; the false-positive rate acts on the healthy group.
Out of 400 healthy people, a test has a 5% false-positive rate (95% specificity). How many false positives does it produce?
Sensitivity measures true hits among the sick; specificity measures true clears among the healthy, and the rest of the healthy group are false positives.

sections.heading: 16.3 Counting inside the positive room
sections.excerpt: 19 out of 68, which is about 27.9%. The 932 people who tested negative are not in the room, so the chance is red divided by red plus amber.

steps.text: Put all 19 truly sick positive testers and all 49 false-positive testers into one room. If you are in that room of 68 people, what is the chance you are actually sick?
19 out of 68, which is about 27.9%. The 932 people who tested negative are not in the room, so the chance is red divided by red plus amber.
In the figure, look at the stacked bar on the far right for 2%, 95% and 5%. The red top piece is 19 and the amber bottom piece is 49, making 68 positive tests in all.

Why did the chance jump from 2% to 27.9%, yet stop far short of 95%? A positive test is 95% ÷ 5% = 19 times as likely when you are sick as when you are healthy, which boosts the odds from 20 : 980 to (20 × 19) : 980 = 380 : 980 = 19 : 49.

The updated probability after seeing the evidence is the posterior. The multiplier sensitivity ÷ false-positive rate (here 95% ÷ 5% = 19) is the likelihood ratio. The rule posterior = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives) is Bayes' theorem.
In a group of 1,000 people, 10 are sick and 990 are healthy. A test flags 9 of the 10 sick people and 9 of the 990 healthy people. By Bayes' theorem, the posterior is 9 ÷ (9 + 9) = 9/18 = 1/2 = 50%.
The tempting slip is to confuse the test's 95% sensitivity with the posterior. Forgetting the base rate and assuming P(sick | +) equals P(+ | sick) is the base-rate trap.
In a screening of 1,000 people, there are 20 true positives and 60 false positives. What is the posterior probability of being sick given a positive test, as a decimal?
Bayes' theorem finds the posterior by dividing true positives by all positives (true positives + false positives), multiplying the prior odds by the likelihood ratio.

debate.title: 90% accurate test: 90% chance or 50% chance?
debate.contextPrompt: Out of 1,000 people, 10 are sick (and 9 test positive) while 990 are healthy (and 9 test positive as false alarms). Asha and Rohan debate the chance a positive tester is sick.
debate.speakerAClaim: 9 out of 10 sick people test positive, so the test is 90% accurate. If you test positive, you have a 90% chance of being sick.
debate.speakerBClaim: 18 people tested positive in all: 9 sick and 9 healthy, in a 1 : 1 ratio. So your chance of being sick is 9 ÷ 18 = 50%.

choices.reasoningStatement: The chance of being sick given a positive test is the same as the test's 90% hit rate.
choices.socraticRebuttal: 90% is the share of sick people who test positive. You also have to count the 9 healthy people who tested positive.

choices.reasoningStatement: Among the 18 people who tested positive, true positives and false positives are in the ratio 9 : 9, so half are sick.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Only 18 people tested positive, 9 sick and 9 healthy, so 9 ÷ 18 = 50%.

choices.reasoningStatement: Divide the 9 sick positive testers by all 1,000 people.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Once you know the test is positive, the 982 people who tested negative are ruled out.

debate.invariantTakeaway: Among all positive tests, compare true positives with false positives: P(sick | +) = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives).

chapters.title: Slopes of curves
chapters.subtitle: Beyond the school book · Zooming in until a curve looks straight, sliding two points together, and finding where a curve levels out
chapters.hookSummary: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A ball thrown into the air slows down, stops at the top, and speeds up on the way down. How do you measure the steepness of a curve at one single instant?

skillCard.skill: Finding the slope of a curve at one point by shrinking the step h to zero, and locating peaks and valleys

sheCan.prompt: With no calculator: for the curve y = x³, what is the derivative dy/dx, and what is the slope of the curve at x = 2? And for the parabola y = x² − 6x + 11, at what value of x is the curve momentarily flat?
sheCan.answer: For y = x³, the power rule brings the 3 down and drops the power by 1: dy/dx = 3x². At x = 2, the slope is 3 × 2² = 12. For y = x² − 6x + 11, the slope is dy/dx = 2x − 6, which equals 0 when x = 3.

skillCard.whyItMatters: Car speedometers, rockets climbing into orbit and businesses finding the best price all rely on the rate of change at one instant.

intuitionToFormula.concreteAction: In the figure, keep the red point at x = 1.25 and slide the step h from 0.45 down toward 0.05.

sections.heading: 17.1 Two points sliding together
sections.excerpt: Pick a second point a small step h to the right, at x = 3 + h. Work out rise ÷ run between them, and watch what number it settles onto as h shrinks toward 0.

steps.text: The gradient rule rise ÷ run needs two points, because dividing 0 ÷ 0 at one point makes no sense. How can we find the slope of the parabola y = x² right at x = 3?
Pick a second point a small step h to the right, at x = 3 + h. Work out rise ÷ run between them, and watch what number it settles onto as h shrinks toward 0.
In the figure, watch the amber line through the two points on the curve as you slide the step h from 0.45 down to 0.05. The amber slope gets closer and closer to the red slope at the first point.
Why does the division work while h is not zero? From x = 3 to x = 3 + h on y = x², the rise is (3 + h)² − 3² = 6h + h². Dividing by h gives 6 + h, and as h shrinks toward 0, 6 + h settles onto 6.

A straight line cutting through two points on a curve is a secant line. The value that an expression approaches as the step shrinks toward zero is the limit. The line that touches the curve at one point with that exact limiting slope is the tangent line.
On y = x² between x = 3 and x = 3.1 (so h = 0.1), the secant line has slope (9.61 − 9) ÷ 0.1 = 6.1. At h = 0.01 it is 6.01, and the limit as h approaches 0 gives a tangent line of slope 6.
The tempting slip is to plug h = 0 in before simplifying, which gives 0 ÷ 0. Expand and divide out h first to get 6 + h, then let h shrink to 0.
On y = x², the secant line from x = 4 to x = 4 + h has slope 8 + h. What is the slope of the tangent line at x = 4 as h shrinks to 0?
A secant line joins two points step h apart; taking the limit as h shrinks to 0 turns it into the tangent line at one point.

sections.heading: 17.2 Speed at a single instant
sections.excerpt: 20 m/s. Over a tiny step of h seconds from t = 2 to t = 2 + h, the distance fallen is 20h + 5h². Dividing by h gives 20 + 5h, which approaches 20 m/s.

steps.text: A stone dropped from a cliff falls y = 5t² metres in t seconds. Between t = 1 and t = 3 it falls 40 metres in 2 seconds, an average of 20 m/s. How fast is it falling at the exact instant t = 2 seconds?
20 m/s. Over a tiny step of h seconds from t = 2 to t = 2 + h, the distance fallen is 20h + 5h². Dividing by h gives 20 + 5h, which approaches 20 m/s.
Draw the curve y = 5t² rising more and more steeply, and draw the straight tangent line touching it at t = 2 with slope 20.
Why does a car's speedometer match the slope of the tangent line? A speedometer measures distance ÷ time over a tiny fraction of a second, which is the tangent slope at that moment.

How fast one quantity changes per unit of another at a single instant is the rate of change. The rule or function that gives the tangent slope at any point x is the derivative, written f′(x) or dy/dx.
For y = 5t², the derivative is dy/dt = 10t. At t = 1 s the stone falls at 10 m/s; at t = 2 s it falls at 20 m/s; at t = 3 s it falls at 30 m/s.

The tempting slip is to divide total height by total time, y ÷ t, as if the graph were a straight line from (0, 0). At t = 2 on y = 5t², y ÷ t gives 20 ÷ 2 = 10 m/s, which is only the average from t = 0 to t = 2, half the instantaneous speed of 20 m/s.
A falling stone has height rule y = 5t² and derivative dy/dt = 10t. What is its instantaneous speed in m/s at t = 4 seconds?
The derivative dy/dx or f′(x) gives the instantaneous rate of change, the slope of the tangent line at x.

sections.heading: 17.3 Why a growing square has two long strips
sections.excerpt: Two long strips, each of area x × h, plus one tiny corner square of area h². Divide the new area 2xh + h² by the step h to get 2x + h, and let h shrink to 0: the derivative of x² is 2x.

steps.text: A square tile has side x and area x². If you widen the square by a thin strip h along its right edge and its top edge, how much new area do you add?
Two long strips, each of area x × h, plus one tiny corner square of area h². Divide the new area 2xh + h² by the step h to get 2x + h, and let h shrink to 0: the derivative of x² is 2x.
Draw a square of side x, and add a strip of width h along the right side and top. Shade the tiny h × h square in the corner.
What happens in 3D when a cube of side x and volume x³ grows by h? It adds three square slabs of face area x² and thickness h, so the derivative of x³ is 3x².
Bringing the exponent n down in front and reducing the exponent by 1 is the power rule. The derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹.
By the power rule, the derivative of x⁴ is 4x³. For y = 3x² + 5x − 7, the derivative is dy/dx = 3(2x) + 5(1) − 0 = 6x + 5, because a constant −7 does not change.
The tempting slip is to bring the power down and forget to subtract 1 from the exponent, writing 3x³ for the derivative of x³. Always drop the exponent by 1: x³ becomes 3x².
Use the power rule to find the derivative dy/dx of y = x³ at x = 2.
The power rule differentiates xⁿ to n xⁿ⁻¹, and a constant term differentiates to 0.

sections.heading: 17.4 Flat at the top of the flight
sections.excerpt: Zero. To change from positive (rising) to negative (falling), a smooth slope must pass through 0 at the top, where the tangent line is horizontal.

steps.text: When you throw a cricket ball straight up, its slope is positive on the way up and negative on the way down. What must its slope be at the exact peak of its flight?
Zero. To change from positive (rising) to negative (falling), a smooth slope must pass through 0 at the top, where the tangent line is horizontal.
Draw a smooth hill and a smooth valley. Lay a ruler flat across the top of the hill and the bottom of the valley.
Why does setting dy/dx = 0 find the peak or the valley? Everywhere else the curve is either still climbing (dy/dx > 0) or already dropping (dy/dx < 0).
A point on a curve where the derivative dy/dx equals 0 is a stationary point. A peak is a local maximum and a valley is a local minimum; together they are maximum and minimum points.
A ball's height is h(t) = 20t − 5t². Its derivative is dh/dt = 20 − 10t. Setting 20 − 10t = 0 gives t = 2 seconds, and the peak height is h(2) = 20(2) − 5(4) = 20 metres.
The tempting slip is to think dy/dx = 0 means the height y is 0. At t = 2 s the slope is 0, while the ball is at its highest point, 20 metres in the air.
For the parabola y = x² − 6x + 11, the derivative is dy/dx = 2x − 6. At what value of x does the curve have its stationary point?
At a stationary point the tangent line is horizontal (dy/dx = 0), marking a smooth maximum and minimum.

debate.title: What does zero slope at the peak mean?
debate.contextPrompt: A cricket ball thrown straight up has height h(t) = 20t − 5t² metres. At t = 2 seconds, its derivative dh/dt is 0. Asha and Rohan debate what dh/dt = 0 tells us.
debate.speakerAClaim: dh/dt = 0 means the ball is at height 0 metres on the ground.
debate.speakerBClaim: At t = 2 seconds the height is 20(2) − 5(4) = 20 metres. dh/dt = 0 means the tangent line is horizontal right at the top of the climb.

choices.reasoningStatement: When the derivative is 0, the height is 0 too.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Substitute t = 2 into 20t − 5t²: 40 − 20 = 20 metres. The derivative measures slope, not height.

choices.speakerLabel: Rohan is right (flat tangent at the 20 m peak)
choices.reasoningStatement: The derivative is the rate of change, which passes through 0 as the ball turns from rising to falling.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. At t = 2 seconds the ball reaches its maximum height of 20 m, where its instantaneous rate of change is 0.

choices.speakerLabel: Neither. The ball floats in the air forever after t = 2.
choices.reasoningStatement: Zero speed means the ball never moves again.
choices.socraticRebuttal: The slope is 0 only at the single instant t = 2; after t = 2, dh/dt = 20 − 10t becomes negative and the ball falls.

debate.invariantTakeaway: At a smooth peak or valley, the derivative dy/dx is 0 because the tangent line is momentarily horizontal.

chapters.title: Areas under curves
chapters.subtitle: Beyond the school book · Slicing a curved region into thin rectangles, running the power rule backwards, and why area undoes slope
chapters.hookSummary: A train's speed graph is a curve, not a flat line. How do you find the exact distance it travelled when the shape under the graph is not a rectangle or a triangle?

skillCard.skill: Approximating the area under a curve with thin rectangles, reversing the power rule to find an antiderivative, and evaluating definite integrals

sheCan.prompt: With no calculator: what is the antiderivative of 2x that is 0 at x = 0? What is the exact area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = 3? Check your answer with the area of a right-angled triangle of base 3 and height 6.
sheCan.answer: The antiderivative of 2x is x², because the derivative of x² is 2x. From x = 0 to x = 3, the area is 3² − 0² = 9, which matches the triangle ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.

skillCard.whyItMatters: Whenever a rate of change varies from moment to moment, the total accumulated change is the area under the rate curve.

sections.heading: 18.1 Slicing a curved shape into thin strips
sections.excerpt: Slice the base into thin strips of equal width Δx. Stand a rectangle on each strip using the height at its middle, and add their areas up.

steps.text: You know how to find the area of a rectangle: width × height. How can rectangles measure the area under a curve whose height keeps changing?
Slice the base into thin strips of equal width Δx. Stand a rectangle on each strip using the height at its middle, and add their areas up.
In the figure, set the upper edge x to 2.4 and slide the number of strips from 4 up to 20. Watch the stepped tops hug the green line more and more closely.
Why measure the height at the midpoint of each strip rather than at its left or right edge? A rising curve is lower on the left and higher on the right, so the missed triangle balances the extra one.
Adding the areas of thin vertical rectangles Σ f(xᵢ) Δx to approximate the area under a curve is a Riemann sum. Choosing the curve's height at the middle of each strip's base is the midpoint rule.
To estimate the area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 2 using 2 strips of width 1, the midpoints are x = 0.5 and x = 1.5. The midpoint rule gives 1 × (0.5)² + 1 × (1.5)² = 0.25 + 2.25 = 2.5.
The tempting slip is to add the heights f(xᵢ) and forget to multiply by the strip width Δx. Each strip is a rectangle, so its area is height × width.
Estimate the area under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = 4 using 2 strips of width 2, with midpoints at x = 1 (height 2) and x = 3 (height 6).
A Riemann sum adds rectangle areas height × width; the midpoint rule takes each height at the middle of its strip.

sections.heading: 18.2 Letting the strips become infinitely thin
sections.excerpt: It moves +30 m forward and −10 m backward, finishing 30 − 10 = 20 m ahead of its start. Area above the time axis adds on; area below the time axis subtracts.

steps.text: A train travels forward at 10 m/s for 3 seconds, then reverses at −5 m/s for 2 seconds. How far from its start does it finish?
It moves +30 m forward and −10 m backward, finishing 30 − 10 = 20 m ahead of its start. Area above the time axis adds on; area below the time axis subtracts.
Draw a rectangle of height +10 and width 3 above the axis (area +30), and a rectangle of depth −5 and width 2 below the axis (area −10).
Why let the number of strips grow without bound on a curved graph? As the strip width dx shrinks to 0, the jagged steps disappear and the limit of the Riemann sum equals the exact area.

The limit of the Riemann sum from x = a to x = b as strip width shrinks to 0 is the definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. The elongated S sign ∫ stands for 'sum'. Because regions above the x-axis count as positive and regions below count as negative, the definite integral measures signed area.
Under y = 2x from x = 0 to x = 3, the region is a triangle of base 3 and height 6. So the definite integral ∫₀³ 2x dx = ½ × 3 × 6 = 9.
The tempting slip is to add the area below the axis instead of subtracting it when finding net change. For signed area, anything below the horizontal axis carries a minus sign.
A curve forms a region of area 14 above the x-axis and a region of area 5 below the x-axis. What is the net signed area (the definite integral across both regions)?
The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the exact limit of the Riemann sum and measures signed area: above the axis minus below.

sections.heading: 18.3 Why slope and area undo each other
sections.excerpt: Each thin strip of area under the speed curve, v(t) × dt, is a tiny step of distance dF. Adding all the tiny steps from t = 1 to t = 4 gives the total change in position: F(4) − F(1) = 4² − 1² = 15.

steps.text: Suppose you know a train's speed at every instant is v(t) = 2t, and you notice that the position rule F(t) = t² has derivative F′(t) = 2t. How can F(t) = t² give you the area under v(t) = 2t from t = 1 to t = 4 in one subtraction?
Each thin strip of area under the speed curve, v(t) × dt, is a tiny step of distance dF. Adding all the tiny steps from t = 1 to t = 4 gives the total change in position: F(4) − F(1) = 4² − 1² = 15.
Stack thin vertical steps dF one on top of another from F(a) up to F(b). The middle steps cancel in pairs, leaving only F(b) − F(a).
How do you reverse the power rule to find F(x) from xⁿ? Differentiating multiplied by the power and subtracted 1; reversing it adds 1 to the power and divides by the new power: xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1).
A function F(x) whose derivative F′(x) equals f(x) is an antiderivative of f(x). The rule that the definite integral of f(x) from a to b equals F(b) − F(a) is the fundamental theorem of calculus.
To find ∫₀² 3x² dx, notice that x³ has derivative 3x², so F(x) = x³ is an antiderivative. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the exact area is F(2) − F(0) = 2³ − 0³ = 8.

The tempting slip when finding an antiderivative of xⁿ is to subtract 1 from the power as if differentiating. Always add 1 to the exponent and divide by the new exponent, then check by differentiating your answer.
Since F(x) = x³ is an antiderivative of 3x², use F(3) − F(1) to find the exact area ∫₁³ 3x² dx.
An antiderivative F(x) reverses the derivative, and the fundamental theorem of calculus says ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

debate.title: What does the area under a speed graph measure?
debate.contextPrompt: A metro train's speed v(t) in m/s is plotted against time t in seconds. Asha and Rohan debate what the area under the v(t) curve represents.
debate.speakerAClaim: The area under the speed graph gives the train's acceleration.
debate.speakerBClaim: Each thin strip has height in m/s multiplied by width in seconds, which gives metres. Adding the strips gives the total distance travelled.

choices.reasoningStatement: Any calculation on a speed graph gives acceleration.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Acceleration is the slope dv/dt, which divides m/s by seconds to get m/s². Area multiplies the two axes.

choices.speakerLabel: Rohan is right (distance travelled in metres)
choices.reasoningStatement: Multiplying height (m/s) by width (s) gives metres for each thin strip, so the total area is total distance.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Slope divides the vertical unit by the horizontal unit; area multiplies them: (m/s) × s = m.

choices.speakerLabel: Neither. It gives the average speed.
choices.reasoningStatement: The area under a curve is its average value.
choices.socraticRebuttal: To get average speed, you would still have to divide that total distance (the area) by the total time.

sections.heading: 19.1 Nose-to-tail journeys and going backwards
sections.excerpt: Walk backwards from A to O, which is (−2, −5), and then forwards from O to B, which is (6, 8). Together that is (6 − 2, 8 − 5) = (4, 3), so AB = OB − OA.

steps.text: From the origin O(0, 0), point A is at (2, 5) and point B is at (6, 8). How do you travel from A to B by going back through O?
Walk backwards from A to O, which is (−2, −5), and then forwards from O to B, which is (6, 8). Together that is (6 − 2, 8 − 5) = (4, 3), so AB = OB − OA.
In the figure, follow the red arrow a from the start, then the blue arrow b from the red tip. The green arrow goes straight from the first tail to the second tip.
Why does AB equal OB − OA and not OA − OB? Starting at A and adding AB lands you at B: OA + AB = OB, so subtracting OA gives AB = OB − OA, 'destination minus start'.

The vector from the origin O to a point A is the position vector of A, written OA or a. Chaining two vectors nose to tail by adding their steps is adding vectors (AB + BC = AC). A journey that finishes where it started, such as AB + BA = (0, 0), gives the zero vector, written 0.
If AB = (4, −2) and BC = (−1, 7), then by adding vectors AC = AB + BC = (4 + (−1), −2 + 7) = (3, 5).
The tempting slip when finding AB from position vectors is to subtract in the order OA − OB. Always do destination minus start: AB = OB − OA.
Point A has position vector OA = (1, 4) and point B has position vector OB = (6, 2). What is the column vector AB = OB − OA?
Position vectors start at O; adding vectors chains them nose to tail (AB + BC = AC), and AB = OB − OA.

sections.heading: 19.2 Length of an arrow and stretching it
sections.excerpt: The 3 m step across and 4 m step up make a right-angled triangle, so the straight-line distance is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 m. And 2a doubles both steps to (6, 8), which is 10 m long in the same direction.

steps.text: A drone flies along the column vector a = (3, 4), moving 3 m East and 4 m North. How far is it in a straight line from its take-off spot, and where does 2a take it?

The 3 m step across and 4 m step up make a right-angled triangle, so the straight-line distance is √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 m. And 2a doubles both steps to (6, 8), which is 10 m long in the same direction.
Draw the right-angled triangle with base 3 and height 4 under the arrow (3, 4), then extend the arrow to twice its length at (6, 8).
Why does (−3)² still give +9 when a component is negative? In v = (5, −12), the step −12 goes downwards, but its length is 12, and (−12)² = +144.
The length of a vector v = (x, y), found by Pythagoras' theorem √(x² + y²), is its magnitude, written |v|. Multiplying both steps of v by a number k gives a scalar multiple, kv = (kx, ky).
For a = (3, 4) and b = (2, −1), the combination 2a − 3b is (6, 8) − (6, −3) = (0, 11), and the magnitude |a| is √(3² + 4²) = 5.
The tempting slip is to think |a + b| equals |a| + |b|. For a = (3, 4) of magnitude 5 and b = (5, −4), the sum a + b is (8, 0) of magnitude 8, which is shorter than the two separate paths.
Find the magnitude |v| of the column vector v = (5, −12).
The magnitude |v| = √(x² + y²) is the arrow's length by Pythagoras, and a scalar multiple kv scales both components by k.

sections.heading: 19.3 Proving two lines are parallel or in one line
sections.excerpt: Write OA = a and OB = b, so AB = b − a. To go from M to N, go ½a back to O and ½b out to N: MN = −½a + ½b = ½(b − a) = ½AB.

steps.text: In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB. How can vectors prove in one line that MN is both parallel to AB and half as long?
Write OA = a and OB = b, so AB = b − a. To go from M to N, go ½a back to O and ½b out to N: MN = −½a + ½b = ½(b − a) = ½AB.
Draw triangle OAB with M halfway along OA and N halfway along OB. Mark AB as b − a and the midsegment MN as ½(b − a).
Why does MN = ½AB prove two geometric facts at once? MN is a scalar multiple of AB, so they are parallel, and the ½ shows MN is half as long.
Points that lie on the same straight line are collinear. If AB is a scalar multiple of BC, they are parallel and share B, so A, B and C are collinear.
If AB = (2, 3) and BC = (6, 9), then BC = 3 × AB. Because BC is a scalar multiple of AB and they share point B, the points A, B and C are collinear.
The tempting slip is to stop after saying 'BC = 3 × AB so they are parallel'. Parallel lines can be separate; you must also state that they share the common point B to prove A, B and C are collinear.
Given AB = (3, −2) and BC = (k, −6), for what value of k are the points A, B and C collinear?
When one vector is a scalar multiple of another they are parallel; if they also share a point, the three points are collinear.

sections.heading: 19.4 Testing for a right angle with the dot product
sections.excerpt: Multiply their x-steps together, multiply their y-steps together, and add: 3 × (−4) + 4 × 3 = −12 + 12 = 0. Whenever that sum is 0 for two non-zero vectors, the angle between them is 90°.

steps.text: Without a grid or protractor, how can you tell in two seconds that u = (3, 4) and v = (−4, 3) meet at 90°?
Multiply their x-steps together, multiply their y-steps together, and add: 3 × (−4) + 4 × 3 = −12 + 12 = 0. Whenever that sum is 0 for two non-zero vectors, the angle between them is 90°.
Draw u = (3, 4) going 3 across and 4 up, and v = (−4, 3) going 4 left and 3 up. The second triangle is the first triangle turned through 90°.
Why does x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ equal 0 at 90°? This formula goes past the school book. By the cosine rule on u, v and u − v, x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ = |u||v| cos θ, and cos 90° = 0.
For u = (x₁, y₁) and v = (x₂, y₂), the number x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ = |u||v| cos θ is the dot product, written u · v. Notice that the dot product of two vectors is a single number (a scalar), not a vector.
For u = (2, 5) and v = (4, −1), the dot product is u · v = (2 × 4) + (5 × (−1)) = 8 − 5 = 3. Since 3 > 0, the angle between them is acute (less than 90°).
The tempting slip is to write the dot product as a column vector (x₁x₂, y₁y₂). Add the two products together so the answer is a single number.
Calculate the dot product u · v of u = (4, 3) and v = (2, −1).
The dot product u · v = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ = |u||v| cos θ is a single number that equals 0 whenever two vectors are perpendicular.

debate.title: Do vector lengths add up directly?
debate.contextPrompt: A drone flies along vector a = (3, 4) of magnitude 5 m, and then along vector b = (5, −4). Asha and Rohan debate the magnitude of the resultant journey a + b.
debate.speakerAClaim: To find the length of a + b, add the two separate lengths together: |a| + |b|.
debate.speakerBClaim: Add the components first: a + b = (3 + 5, 4 − 4) = (8, 0). The +4 North and −4 South cancel out, leaving a straight 8 m journey East.

choices.speakerLabel: Asha is right (add the two lengths)
choices.reasoningStatement: The magnitude of a sum is the sum of the magnitudes.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Lengths add directly only when both vectors point in the exact same direction. Here the second leg turns back South.

choices.speakerLabel: Rohan is right (a + b = (8, 0), magnitude 8 m)
choices.reasoningStatement: Vectors add nose to tail by their horizontal and vertical steps, and the straight shortcut is shorter than the detour.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Adding components gives (3 + 5, 4 − 4) = (8, 0), which has magnitude 8 m.

choices.speakerLabel: Neither. Multiply the components to get (15, −16).
choices.reasoningStatement: Combining two vectors multiplies their steps.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Walking 3 m East and then 5 m East puts you 3 + 5 = 8 m East, not 15 m.

debate.invariantTakeaway: Add vectors by their components nose to tail first, then find the magnitude of the resultant vector.

sheCan.prompt: With no calculator: for the 2×2 matrix A = [[3, 1], [2, 4]], where does it send the vector (2, 1)? What is its determinant det(A) = ad − bc, and what does A do to the area of a triangle of area 5 cm²?
sheCan.answer: A sends (2, 1) to 2 × (3, 2) + 1 × (1, 4) = (6 + 1, 4 + 4) = (7, 8). Its determinant is (3 × 4) − (1 × 2) = 12 − 2 = 10, so the triangle's area becomes 10 × 5 = 50 cm².
