sections.heading: 20.1 Two arrows that move the whole grid
sections.excerpt: It must land at 2 lots of (3, 2) plus 1 lot of (1, 4), which is (6, 4) + (1, 4) = (7, 8). Knowing where the two unit arrows land tells you where every point on the plane lands.

steps.text: Every point (x, y) is x steps of (1, 0) plus y steps of (0, 1). If a grid move sends (1, 0) to (3, 2) and (0, 1) to (1, 4), where must the point (2, 1) land?
It must land at 2 lots of (3, 2) plus 1 lot of (1, 4), which is (6, 4) + (1, 4) = (7, 8). Knowing where the two unit arrows land tells you where every point on the plane lands.
Draw the red unit arrow (1, 0) and the blue unit arrow (0, 1). Watch them land at (3, 2) and (1, 4), carrying the whole grid with them.

Why do those two arrows control the whole grid? When grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced and (0, 0) stays put, 2 steps across and 1 step up must become 2 red arrows plus 1 blue arrow.

The unit step across î = (1, 0) and unit step up ĵ = (0, 1) are the basis vectors. A move of the plane that keeps grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced with the origin fixed is a linear transformation. Writing the landed red arrow (a, c) and blue arrow (b, d) as two columns makes a 2×2 matrix, [[a, b], [c, d]].
The matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]] has first column (2, 0) and second column (0, 3). It stretches every x-coordinate by 2 and every y-coordinate by 3, sending (4, 5) to (8, 15).
The tempting slip is to read the rows of [[3, 1], [2, 4]] as the two landed arrows. Read down the columns: column 1 is (3, 2) where î lands, and column 2 is (1, 4) where ĵ lands.
A linear transformation sends î = (1, 0) to (4, 1) and ĵ = (0, 1) to (2, 3). Where does it send the vector (1, 2)?
A 2×2 matrix records where the basis vectors î and ĵ land in its two columns, sending (x, y) to x × (column 1) + y × (column 2).

sections.heading: 20.2 Doing one transformation after another
sections.excerpt: No. Follow the basis vector î = (1, 0): reflecting in the x-axis keeps it at (1, 0), and rotating 90° sends it to (0, 1). In the reverse order, rotating 90° sends (1, 0) to (0, 1), and reflecting in the x-axis flips that to (0, −1).

steps.text: First reflect a shape across the x-axis, then rotate it 90° anticlockwise. Do you get the same result if you rotate first and reflect second?

No. Follow the basis vector î = (1, 0): reflecting in the x-axis keeps it at (1, 0), and rotating 90° sends it to (0, 1). In the reverse order, rotating 90° sends (1, 0) to (0, 1), and reflecting in the x-axis flips that to (0, −1).
Hold a book flat on the desk: flip it left-to-right then turn it 90° clockwise; now start again, turn it 90° clockwise first, then flip it left-to-right. The cover ends up facing a different way.
How do we combine matrix B followed by matrix A into one matrix AB? Apply A to B's first column, then apply A to B's second column.
Combining two linear transformations by letting the left matrix act on each column of the right matrix is matrix multiplication. Each entry of AB is a row-by-column dot product, and usually AB ≠ BA.
The tempting slip is to multiply the four numbers in matching positions, top-left by top-left. Instead, multiply each row of the left matrix by each column of the right matrix.
Multiply the matrix [[2, 1], [0, 3]] by the column vector (4, 2).
Matrix multiplication applies the left matrix to each column of the right matrix, and the order of multiplication matters.

sections.heading: 20.3 Why the area of the parallelogram is ad − bc
sections.excerpt: ad − bc. Fit the parallelogram inside an (a + b) by (c + d) rectangle of area ac + ad + bc + bd. Subtract four corner triangles (area ac + bd) and two b × c rectangles (area 2bc) to leave ad − bc.

steps.text: The matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] turns the 1 × 1 unit square into a tilted parallelogram spanned by (a, c) and (b, d). What is the area of that parallelogram?
ad − bc. Fit the parallelogram inside an (a + b) by (c + d) rectangle of area ac + ad + bc + bd. Subtract four corner triangles (area ac + bd) and two b × c rectangles (area 2bc) to leave ad − bc.
In the figure, set a = 2, b = 1 and d = 2. The amber parallelogram between (2, 1) and (1, 2) has area 2(2) − 1(1) = 3.
What happens when the two columns point along the same line, such as (2, 1) and (4, 2)? The parallelogram squashes flat onto a single line with zero width, and ad − bc = 2(2) − 4(1) = 0.

The signed area scale factor of a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] is its determinant, written det(A) = ad − bc. A matrix whose determinant is 0 squashes 2D space onto a line (or a point) and cannot be undone; it is called a singular matrix.
For A = [[3, 1], [2, 4]], det(A) = (3 × 4) − (1 × 2) = 12 − 2 = 10. Because every unit square is multiplied in area by 10, a triangle of area 5 cm² is transformed to area 10 × 5 = 50 cm².

The tempting slip is to add the products ad + bc instead of subtracting ad − bc. Test the identity matrix [[1, 0], [0, 1]] or two equal columns [[1, 1], [1, 1]]: equal columns must collapse to area 1 − 1 = 0.
Calculate the determinant det(A) = ad − bc of the matrix A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]].
The determinant det(A) = ad − bc tells you how many times bigger every area becomes; when det(A) = 0, the matrix is singular.

sections.heading: 20.4 Arrows that stretch without turning
sections.excerpt: A sends (1, 1) to (2×1 + 1×1, 1×1 + 2×1) = (3, 3), which is 3 × (1, 1). It stays on the exact same 45° line and stretches to 3 times its length.

steps.text: When the matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] stretches the plane, most vectors get knocked off their starting line. What happens to the diagonal vector v = (1, 1)?
A sends (1, 1) to (2×1 + 1×1, 1×1 + 2×1) = (3, 3), which is 3 × (1, 1). It stays on the exact same 45° line and stretches to 3 times its length.
Draw the two diagonal lines y = x through (1, 1) and y = −x through (1, −1). Under [[2, 1], [1, 2]], the first diagonal stretches by 3 and the second diagonal stays at 1 × (1, −1).
Why do we care about the directions that do not turn? Along those two axes, the matrix stretches by 3 in one direction and 1 in the other, scaling area by 3 × 1 = 3.
A non-zero vector v that a matrix A stretches without turning, so that Av = λv, is an eigenvector of A. The scale factor λ (the Greek letter lambda) is its eigenvalue.
For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] and v = (1, −1), multiplying gives Av = (2 − 1, 1 − 2) = (1, −1) = 1 × v. So (1, −1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ = 1.
The tempting slip is to call the zero vector (0, 0) an eigenvector because A(0, 0) = (0, 0). The zero vector has no direction to keep; an eigenvector must be a non-zero vector.
The matrix A = [[4, 2], [1, 3]] sends the eigenvector v = (2, 1) to Av = (10, 5). Since (10, 5) = λ(2, 1), what is the eigenvalue λ?
An eigenvector v stays on its own line when multiplied by A (Av = λv), and the stretch factor λ is its eigenvalue.

debate.title: When every entry is positive, can the area still be zero?
debate.contextPrompt: The matrix A = [[2, 4], [1, 2]] transforms the 1 × 1 unit square. Asha and Rohan debate the area of the transformed shape.
debate.speakerAClaim: Every number in [[2, 4], [1, 2]] is positive and at least 1, so the unit square must stretch into a bigger parallelogram.
debate.speakerBClaim: Column 2 is (4, 2), which is 2 times column 1, (2, 1). Both basis vectors land on the same line, so det(A) = 2(2) − 4(1) = 0 and the area collapses to 0.

choices.reasoningStatement: Positive matrix entries always expand area.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Plot the two columns (2, 1) and (4, 2): both have gradient 1/2, so there is zero width between them.

choices.reasoningStatement: When one column is a scalar multiple of the other, the 2D square squashes flat onto a 1D line of area 0.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Yes. Because (4, 2) = 2 × (2, 1), both basis arrows lie on the line y = ½x, and det(A) = 4 − 4 = 0.

choices.reasoningStatement: Subtracting bc makes the area negative.
choices.socraticRebuttal: Here ad = 4 and bc = 4, so ad − bc = 4 − 4 = 0.

debate.invariantTakeaway: The determinant det(A) = ad − bc measures the area scale factor; if one column is a multiple of the other, det(A) = 0.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 0 · Two circles in a class of 30
atlasLessons.question: Why do 18 cricket players and 15 football players make only 26 students who play a sport?
atlasLessons.explanation: The 7 who play both are inside both counts. Take them away once: 18 + 15 − 7 = 26.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
stories: How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 0 · Outside both circles
atlasLessons.question: How many of the 30 students play neither sport?
atlasLessons.explanation: 26 play at least one sport, so 30 − 26 = 4 are outside both circles. They make up the complement of A ∪ B.
atlasLessons.limits: The count: n((A ∪ B)′) = 30 − 26 = 4
stories: How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 0 · Not this and not that
atlasLessons.question: Why is outside A ∪ B the same as outside A and outside B?
atlasLessons.explanation: To be outside the union, a student must miss both sports. Missing one is not enough. So (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′.
atlasLessons.limits: De Morgan's law: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′
stories: How do you count a crowd without counting anyone twice?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · Turning round on the number line
atlasLessons.question: What does multiplying by −1 do to a number?
atlasLessons.explanation: It keeps the size and turns the direction round. 3 becomes −3, and −3 becomes 3.
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · What two numbers share
atlasLessons.question: How do the HCF and the LCM of 24 and 36 come from their prime factors?
atlasLessons.explanation: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. The shared primes give the HCF, 12. Every prime either number needs gives the LCM, 72.
atlasLessons.limits: The check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 1 · Why the check always works
atlasLessons.question: Why does HCF × LCM equal the two numbers multiplied together?
atlasLessons.explanation: 24 × 36 uses every prime of both numbers. The LCM takes each prime the most times it appears in either number. The HCF takes the shared ones, which are exactly the primes the LCM left out. Between them they use every prime once.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: HCF × LCM = a × b
stories: Why does a minus times a minus make a plus?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 2 · Lining up the repeating digits
atlasLessons.question: Why does multiplying 0.3636… by 100 help to turn it into a fraction?
atlasLessons.explanation: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left. The digits after the point still read 3636…, as they did before. Subtracting the original number removes them all and leaves the whole number 36.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 99 × the number = 36, so the number is 4/11
stories: How can 0.333… go on for ever and still be exactly one third?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 2 · How many pieces fit?
atlasLessons.question: Why is dividing by 2/3 the same as multiplying by 3/2?
atlasLessons.explanation: Cutting each whole into thirds multiplies the count by 3. Grouping the thirds in twos divides it by 2. Doing both is multiplying by 3/2.
stories: How can 0.333… go on for ever and still be exactly one third?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 2 · The decimal that is secretly 1
atlasLessons.question: What fraction is 0.999…?
atlasLessons.explanation: Ten lots of it are 9.999…, and one lot is 0.999…, with the same tail. Take one lot from ten lots and nine lots are exactly 9. So the number is 9/9, which is 1. 0.999… and 1 are two names for one number.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 0.999… = 1
stories: How can 0.333… go on for ever and still be exactly one third?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 3 · Sharing in a ratio
atlasLessons.question: Why do you add the parts of a ratio before you share?
atlasLessons.explanation: The amount is cut into equal parts, and the ratio says how many parts each person takes. Adding tells you how many parts there are in all. Dividing by that number gives the size of one part.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: 1 part = total ÷ number of parts
stories: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 3 · Up 20%, then down 20%
atlasLessons.question: Why does a 20% rise followed by a 20% fall leave you with less?
atlasLessons.explanation: The rise multiplies by 1.2 and the fall multiplies by 0.8. Together they multiply by 0.96. The fall is 20% of the bigger amount, so it takes off more than the rise put on.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% fall
stories: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 3 · The doubling rule
atlasLessons.question: Why does money at 8% a year double in about 9 years?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each year multiplies the money by 1.08. Nine of those multiplications come to almost exactly 2. The rule of 72 finds the 9 without the long sum: 72 ÷ 8 = 9.
atlasLessons.limits: The result: 1.08 multiplied nine times is about 2
stories: A price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Why is it not back where it started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 4 · Multiplying out a bracket
atlasLessons.question: Why does the number outside a bracket multiply every term inside?
atlasLessons.explanation: A bracket is one amount, so 4(x + 3) means four lots of x + 3. Four lots hold four x's and four 3s, which is 4x + 12.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: a(b + c) = ab + ac
stories: A square tile of side x grows by 3 cm along each edge. Why is its new area not x² + 9?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 4 · Two brackets
atlasLessons.question: Why does (x + 3)(x + 2) have four pieces?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each bracket is one side of a rectangle, cut into two lengths. Two lengths along the top and two down the side make four pieces. They are x², 3x, 2x and 6, and the two strips join to make 5x.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab
stories: A square tile of side x grows by 3 cm along each edge. Why is its new area not x² + 9?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 4 · The corner cut away
atlasLessons.question: Why is 53² − 47² the same as 6 × 100?
atlasLessons.explanation: Cut a 47 by 47 square from the corner of a 53 by 53 square. The L-shape left over rearranges into a rectangle 6 wide and 100 long.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)
stories: A square tile of side x grows by 3 cm along each edge. Why is its new area not x² + 9?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 5 · The same to both sides
atlasLessons.question: Why does doing the same thing to both sides keep an equation true?
atlasLessons.explanation: An equation says two amounts are equal, like the two pans of a level balance. Change both by the same amount, and they are still equal. Change one only, and the balance tips.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: ax + b = c gives x = (c − b) ÷ a
stories: 4 bags of marbles and 3 loose marbles balance 15 marbles. How many marbles are in a bag, without opening one?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 5 · Turning a formula round
atlasLessons.question: Why do you undo the steps of a formula in reverse order?
atlasLessons.explanation: A formula builds its subject in steps, such as × 12 and then + 50. The last step done sits on the outside, so it comes off first.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: C = 50 + 12d gives d = (C − 50) ÷ 12
stories: 4 bags of marbles and 3 loose marbles balance 15 marbles. How many marbles are in a bag, without opening one?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 5 · When the sign turns round
atlasLessons.question: Why does dividing by a negative number turn an inequality round?
atlasLessons.explanation: Multiplying by −1 reflects every number across 0. The number that was further right lands further left, so the bigger one becomes the smaller one.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: if a < b, then −a > −b
stories: 4 bags of marbles and 3 loose marbles balance 15 marbles. How many marbles are in a bag, without opening one?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 6 · Equal steps
atlasLessons.question: How can you tell whether a list of numbers goes up in equal steps?
atlasLessons.explanation: Take each term away from the next one. If every gap is the same, the list is an arithmetic sequence and that gap is its common difference.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: equal gaps d give the nth term dn + c
stories: A row of 10 squares made of matchsticks needs 31 matches, not 40. How many does a row of 100 squares need, without counting?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 6 · Jumping to the 100th term
atlasLessons.question: Why does the number in front of n match the gap between terms?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each step along the list adds the same gap d. After n steps, the gaps add up to dn, and a fixed number corrects the start.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d
stories: A row of 10 squares made of matchsticks needs 31 matches, not 40. How many does a row of 100 squares need, without counting?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 6 · Two staircases make a rectangle
atlasLessons.question: Why is 1 + 2 + … + n half of n × (n + 1)?
atlasLessons.explanation: Turn a copy of the staircase upside down and set it on top. Every column then reaches n + 1, so the two staircases fill a rectangle n by n + 1.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1) ÷ 2
stories: A row of 10 squares made of matchsticks needs 31 matches, not 40. How many does a row of 100 squares need, without counting?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 7 · Rise over run
atlasLessons.question: Why does the gradient of a straight line not depend on where you measure it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Any step under a straight line makes a triangle of the same shape. A step twice as wide rises twice as far, so the rise divided by the run never changes.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: gradient = change in y ÷ change in x
stories: A taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for every kilometre. Mark the fares for 0 to 4 km as dots on squared paper. Why do the dots fall in a straight row?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 7 · Reading y = mx + c
atlasLessons.question: How can you see a line's steepness and its starting point in its equation?
atlasLessons.explanation: Put x = 0 and y is c, so the line crosses the y-axis at (0, c). Each step of 1 across adds m to y, so m is the gradient.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: y = mx + c
stories: A taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for every kilometre. Mark the fares for 0 to 4 km as dots on squared paper. Why do the dots fall in a straight row?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 7 · Speed is a gradient
atlasLessons.question: On a distance-time graph, why does a steeper line mean a faster trip?
atlasLessons.explanation: The gradient is the distance covered divided by the time taken, which is the speed. A flat line covers no distance, so it means standing still.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: speed = distance ÷ time
stories: A taxi costs ₹50 to start and ₹20 for every kilometre. Mark the fares for 0 to 4 km as dots on squared paper. Why do the dots fall in a straight row?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 8 · Parallel lines keep their angles
atlasLessons.question: Why are corresponding angles equal when the lines are parallel?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slide one parallel line along the transversal onto the other. It moves without turning, so every angle at the first crossing lands on the matching angle at the second.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°
stories: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and lay them side by side, points touching. They make a straight line every time. Why does that work for every triangle?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 8 · One proof for every triangle
atlasLessons.question: How can one drawing show that the angles of every triangle add to 180°?
atlasLessons.explanation: Draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. Alternate angles copy the other two corners onto that line, and a straight line is 180°.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: the angles of a triangle add to 180°
stories: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and lay them side by side, points touching. They make a straight line every time. Why does that work for every triangle?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 8 · Cutting a polygon into triangles
atlasLessons.question: Why do the interior angles of an n-sided polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°?
atlasLessons.explanation: Lines from one corner cut the polygon into triangles, two fewer than it has sides. The angles of those triangles fill its corners, 180° for each triangle.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: the interior angles of an n-sided polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°
stories: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and lay them side by side, points touching. They make a straight line every time. Why does that work for every triangle?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 9 · Two arcs and a fold
atlasLessons.question: Why does the line through two equal arc crossings cut AB in half at a right angle?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each crossing is the same distance from A as from B. Fold the page along the line through them and A lands on B, so the fold meets AB at its midpoint.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: the perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equally far from A and B
stories: With only a pencil, a ruler and a pair of compasses you can cut a line exactly in half. No measuring is needed. Why do two arcs know where the middle is?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 9 · Turning round on a bearing
atlasLessons.question: Why does a back bearing differ from the bearing by 180°?
atlasLessons.explanation: The north arrows at the start and at the finish are parallel. The path back points the opposite way, and opposite directions are half a turn apart.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: back bearing = bearing ± 180°, written with three figures
stories: With only a pencil, a ruler and a pair of compasses you can cut a line exactly in half. No measuring is needed. Why do two arcs know where the middle is?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 9 · Vertices minus edges plus faces
atlasLessons.question: Why does V − E + F come to 2 for a cube and for a pyramid alike?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slicing a corner off a solid adds 2 vertices, 3 edges and 1 face. So V − E + F changes by 2 − 3 + 1 = 0, and it stays at 2.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: V − E + F = 2 for a solid with flat faces and no holes
stories: With only a pencil, a ruler and a pair of compasses you can cut a line exactly in half. No measuring is needed. Why do two arcs know where the middle is?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 10 · A circle laid out flat
atlasLessons.question: Why is the area of a circle πr²?
atlasLessons.explanation: Cut the circle into thin slices and lay them top to tail. The strip is half the circumference long, πr, and one radius tall, so it covers πr × r.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: the area of a circle is πr², and its circumference is 2πr
stories: A circle has no straight sides to measure along. So how can a pizza's area be worked out with a ruler?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 10 · Two trapeziums side by side
atlasLessons.question: Why is a trapezium's area half of (a + b) × h?
atlasLessons.explanation: Two copies of the trapezium, one turned over, make a parallelogram a + b long and h tall. One trapezium is half of that parallelogram.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: the area of a trapezium is ½(a + b) × h, with h at a right angle to the parallel sides
stories: A circle has no straight sides to measure along. So how can a pizza's area be worked out with a ruler?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 10 · Slices that add up
atlasLessons.question: Why is a prism's volume the area of its cross-section times its length?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each 1 cm slice along the prism holds as many cubes as the cross-section has squares. Count the slices and multiply.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: volume of a prism = area of the cross-section × length
stories: A circle has no straight sides to measure along. So how can a pizza's area be worked out with a ruler?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 11 · Lines from the centre
atlasLessons.question: Why does an enlargement keep a shape's angles?
atlasLessons.explanation: Every corner moves along its own line from the centre, to k times as far. Every side is multiplied by k, so the shape stays the same, only bigger or smaller.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: an enlargement with scale factor k multiplies every length by k
stories: A torch makes a shadow of a cut-out triangle, twice as tall on the wall. Is the shadow's area twice as big too?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 11 · Moves that keep the size
atlasLessons.question: Why do a translation, a reflection and a rotation never change an area?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each one moves every point but keeps the distance between any two points. The image is congruent to the object, so its area is the same.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: translations, reflections and rotations give congruent images
stories: A torch makes a shadow of a cut-out triangle, twice as tall on the wall. Is the shadow's area twice as big too?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 11 · Copies inside the image
atlasLessons.question: Why does scale factor 3 make an area 9 times as big?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each length is 3 times as long, across and up at once. So 3 × 3 = 9 copies of the shape fit inside the image.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: lengths × k, areas × k², volumes × k³
stories: A torch makes a shadow of a cut-out triangle, twice as tall on the wall. Is the shadow's area twice as big too?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 12 · The squares on a right-angled triangle
atlasLessons.question: Why do the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the hypotenuse?
atlasLessons.explanation: Four copies of the triangle fit round a tilted square inside a bigger square. Moved around, they leave two smaller squares uncovered instead, with the same area.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: a² + b² = c² works only when the angle between a and b is 90°
stories: A ladder 5 m long leans on a wall, with its foot 3 m out. How high up the wall does it reach, without climbing it?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 12 · Ratios that belong to an angle
atlasLessons.question: Why is sin 30° the same in a set square and in a mountain?
atlasLessons.explanation: Any two right-angled triangles with a 30° angle are similar shapes. One is an enlargement of the other, so height ÷ hypotenuse is the same in both.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: sin θ, cos θ and tan θ depend only on the angle θ
stories: A ladder 5 m long leans on a wall, with its foot 3 m out. How high up the wall does it reach, without climbing it?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 12 · The point on the circle
atlasLessons.question: Why is the point at angle θ on the unit circle at (cos θ, sin θ)?
atlasLessons.explanation: Its radius is 1 and is the hypotenuse of the triangle under it. Height ÷ 1 is sin θ and across ÷ 1 is cos θ.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 at every angle
stories: A ladder 5 m long leans on a wall, with its foot 3 m out. How high up the wall does it reach, without climbing it?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 13 · Fair shares in a stratified sample
atlasLessons.question: Why do we multiply the sample size by each group's fraction of the population?
atlasLessons.explanation: If a year group holds 240 out of 600 students, it is two fifths of the school. Giving it two fifths of the sample means every student in the school has the same chance of being chosen.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: group sample = (group size ÷ total population) × sample size
stories: A soup pot holds 10 litres. You do not drink all 10 litres to check the salt. You stir the pot well and taste one spoonful.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 13 · Seeing the missing data
atlasLessons.question: Why does a huge sample still lie when the method has bias?
atlasLessons.explanation: If a survey leaves out one part of the population, taking more replies from the same place repeats the same blind spot.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: a random or stratified choice comes before sample size
stories: A soup pot holds 10 litres. You do not drink all 10 litres to check the salt. You stir the pot well and taste one spoonful.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 13 · The square-root law of sample size
atlasLessons.question: Why must you quadruple the sample size to cut the standard error in half?
atlasLessons.explanation: Random ups and downs cancel in proportion to √n. Dividing by √(4n) is dividing by 2√n, which halves the typical error.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: standard error = σ ÷ √n
stories: A soup pot holds 10 litres. You do not drink all 10 litres to check the salt. You stir the pot well and taste one spoonful.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 14 · Why unequal widths need frequency density
atlasLessons.question: Why can't we plot the raw count as the bar height when class widths differ?
atlasLessons.explanation: A class that is twice as wide collects items across twice the span. Dividing count by class width gives the rate per unit width, so the rectangle's area equals the count.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: frequency density = count ÷ class width
stories: Two bus routes both take 20 minutes on average. One arrives in 19, 20 or 21 minutes; the other takes 5 minutes or 35. The average alone hides the wait.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 14 · Median and interquartile range
atlasLessons.question: Why do we use the median and interquartile range when a list has an extreme outlier?
atlasLessons.explanation: One huge value pulls the mean and standard deviation toward it, but the median and the middle half between Q₁ and Q₃ barely move.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ covers the middle 50% of the ordered list
stories: Two bus routes both take 20 minutes on average. One arrives in 19, 20 or 21 minutes; the other takes 5 minutes or 35. The average alone hides the wait.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 14 · Squaring the gaps for standard deviation
atlasLessons.question: Why do we square each distance from the mean before averaging?
atlasLessons.explanation: Gaps below the mean are negative and gaps above are positive, so they add to zero. Squaring makes every term positive, and the square root at the end restores the original unit.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n, and standard deviation σ = √variance
stories: Two bus routes both take 20 minutes on average. One arrives in 19, 20 or 21 minutes; the other takes 5 minutes or 35. The average alone hides the wait.

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 15 · Why sample-space grids keep outcomes fair
atlasLessons.question: Why does a 6 × 6 grid give the right dice probabilities when listing totals 2 to 12 does not?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each of the 36 squares pairs one face of the first die with one face of the second die, so all 36 squares are equally likely.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: P(A) = wanted squares ÷ total equally likely squares
stories: Roll two fair dice and add the spots. Why does a total of 7 show up six times as often as a total of 12?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 15 · Multiplying along tree branches
atlasLessons.question: When do the branch fractions stay the same on the second step of a tree?
atlasLessons.explanation: They stay the same when the two steps are independent events, such as tossing a coin twice or drawing with replacement.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events
stories: Roll two fair dice and add the spots. Why does a total of 7 show up six times as often as a total of 12?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 15 · Dividing out the order
atlasLessons.question: Why does ⁿCᵣ divide the ordered count ⁿPᵣ by r!?
atlasLessons.explanation: Every team of r people can be lined up in r! different orders. Dividing by r! collapses those r! orders into one single team.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿPᵣ ÷ r! = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!)
stories: Roll two fair dice and add the spots. Why does a total of 7 show up six times as often as a total of 12?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 16 · Why the base rate matters
atlasLessons.question: Why does a 95% accurate test give so many false alarms when a condition is rare?
atlasLessons.explanation: When only 20 in 1,000 people have the condition, 980 are healthy. Even a 5% false-alarm rate on 980 healthy people creates 49 false positives, more than twice the 19 true positives.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: count true positives and false positives out of 1,000 people first
stories: A medical test is 95% accurate, and you test positive for a condition that affects 2 in 100 people. Why is the chance you actually have it only about 28%, not 95%?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 16 · Throwing away the negative tests
atlasLessons.question: Why is the denominator 68 instead of 1,000 once the test comes back positive?
atlasLessons.explanation: The 932 people who tested negative are no longer possible cases. Conditioning on a positive test restricts the world to the 19 + 49 = 68 positive testers.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: P(D | +) = TP ÷ (TP + FP)
stories: A medical test is 95% accurate, and you test positive for a condition that affects 2 in 100 people. Why is the chance you actually have it only about 28%, not 95%?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 16 · Multiplying the odds by the likelihood ratio
atlasLessons.question: How does a positive test change the ratio of sick to healthy?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each sick person is 95% ÷ 5% = 19 times as likely to test positive as each healthy person. So the prior ratio 20 : 980 is multiplied by 19 to become 380 : 980 = 19 : 49.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio
stories: A medical test is 95% accurate, and you test positive for a condition that affects 2 in 100 people. Why is the chance you actually have it only about 28%, not 95%?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 17 · From secant slope to tangent slope
atlasLessons.question: How do we find the slope at one point when the gradient formula needs two points?
atlasLessons.explanation: Take a second point at x + h and simplify the secant slope while h is not zero. Then take the limit as h shrinks to 0.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: f′(x) = limit as h → 0 of (f(x + h) − f(x)) ÷ h
stories: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A ball thrown into the air slows down, stops at the top, and speeds up on the way down. How do you measure the steepness of a curve at one single instant?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 17 · The geometry of the power rule
atlasLessons.question: Why does the derivative of x² have a 2 in front, and the derivative of x³ have a 3?
atlasLessons.explanation: A square grows along 2 edges of length x, and a cube grows along 3 square faces of area x². The tiny corner pieces have h² or h³ and vanish when divided by h as h → 0.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: d/dx(xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
stories: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A ball thrown into the air slows down, stops at the top, and speeds up on the way down. How do you measure the steepness of a curve at one single instant?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 17 · Finding peaks and valleys
atlasLessons.question: Why does setting the derivative to 0 locate a smooth maximum or minimum?
atlasLessons.explanation: A smooth curve climbs before a peak and falls after it. At the turning point between rising and falling, the tangent line is horizontal (slope 0).
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: stationary points occur where f′(x) = 0
stories: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A ball thrown into the air slows down, stops at the top, and speeds up on the way down. How do you measure the steepness of a curve at one single instant?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 18 · Adding thin rectangles
atlasLessons.question: Why does the midpoint rule give a closer estimate than using the left or right edge of each strip?
atlasLessons.explanation: At the midpoint of a strip, a rising curve lies below the top on the left and above it on the right. The two small triangular errors cancel.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: Riemann sum = Σ f(xᵢ) Δx
stories: A train's speed graph is a curve, not a flat line. How do you find the exact distance it travelled when the shape under the graph is not a rectangle or a triangle?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 18 · Reversing the power rule
atlasLessons.question: How do we find an antiderivative of xⁿ?
atlasLessons.explanation: Since differentiating multiplies by the exponent and subtracts 1, reversing it adds 1 to the exponent and divides by the new exponent: xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1).
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: an antiderivative of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1)
stories: A train's speed graph is a curve, not a flat line. How do you find the exact distance it travelled when the shape under the graph is not a rectangle or a triangle?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 18 · The fundamental theorem of calculus
atlasLessons.question: Why does the area under f(x) from a to b equal F(b) − F(a)?
atlasLessons.explanation: Each thin strip of area f(x) dx equals a small rise dF on the antiderivative curve F(x). Adding all the small rises from x = a to x = b gives the total height change F(b) − F(a).
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F′(x) = f(x)
stories: A train's speed graph is a curve, not a flat line. How do you find the exact distance it travelled when the shape under the graph is not a rectangle or a triangle?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 19 · Why vectors add nose to tail
atlasLessons.question: Why do we add the x-steps and y-steps separately when chaining two vectors?
atlasLessons.explanation: A step of x₁ East followed by x₂ East puts you x₁ + x₂ East. A step of y₁ North followed by y₂ North puts you y₁ + y₂ North.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: (x₁, y₁) + (x₂, y₂) = (x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂)
stories: Walk 3 steps East and 4 steps North, then 2 steps East and 1 step South. Where do you finish, and how far in a straight line are you from where you started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 19 · Proving geometry with scalar multiples
atlasLessons.question: How does showing u = kv prove two lines are parallel?
atlasLessons.explanation: Multiplying both steps of v by k scales the length by |k| while keeping the slope y ÷ x unchanged. So u and v share the same direction.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: u = kv means u is parallel to v and |k| times as long
stories: Walk 3 steps East and 4 steps North, then 2 steps East and 1 step South. Where do you finish, and how far in a straight line are you from where you started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 19 · The dot product and right angles
atlasLessons.question: Why is the dot product u · v equal to 0 when two vectors are perpendicular?
atlasLessons.explanation: The dot product measures |u||v| cos θ, the length of one vector multiplied by the shadow of the other along it. At 90° a vector casts zero shadow along the line perpendicular to it.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: u · v = x₁x₂ + y₁y₂ = 0 at 90°
stories: Walk 3 steps East and 4 steps North, then 2 steps East and 1 step South. Where do you finish, and how far in a straight line are you from where you started?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 20 · Reading a matrix by its columns
atlasLessons.question: Why do the two columns of a 2×2 matrix tell you where every point (x, y) goes?
atlasLessons.explanation: Every vector (x, y) is x î + y ĵ. A linear transformation keeps sums and scalar multiples, so (x, y) lands at x × (column 1) + y × (column 2).
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: [[a, b], [c, d]] (x, y) = (ax + by, cx + dy)
stories: When you pinch-zoom or rotate a photo on a screen, the tablet moves millions of pixels at once. How can four numbers tell every point on the grid where to land?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 20 · Subtracting the corners for ad − bc
atlasLessons.question: Why is the area of the parallelogram spanned by (a, c) and (b, d) equal to ad − bc?
atlasLessons.explanation: It fits inside an (a + b) by (c + d) bounding box. Subtracting the four right-angled triangles around the edges (area ac + bd) and the two b × c corner rectangles (area 2bc) leaves ad − bc.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: det([[a, b], [c, d]]) = ad − bc
stories: When you pinch-zoom or rotate a photo on a screen, the tablet moves millions of pixels at once. How can four numbers tell every point on the grid where to land?

atlasLessons.title: Chapter 20 · Eigenvectors as the steady axes of a transformation
atlasLessons.question: What makes an eigenvector different from other vectors when a matrix acts on the plane?
atlasLessons.explanation: Most vectors both stretch and turn when multiplied by A. An eigenvector v stays on its own line, so Av = λv.
atlasLessons.limits: The rule: Av = λv for a non-zero eigenvector v
stories: When you pinch-zoom or rotate a photo on a screen, the tablet moves millions of pixels at once. How can four numbers tell every point on the grid where to land?

widgets.title: Two circles in a class of 30
widgets.challengePrompt: Put 18 in A, 15 in B and 7 in both. Predict how many students are outside both circles, then read the figure.
widgets.cutaway: 11 play cricket only, 7 play both and 8 play football only. That is 26, so 4 are outside both circles.
widgets.idealised: The rule: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Put 18 in A, 15 in B and 7 in both.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The four parts are 11, 7, 8 and 4. Together they make 30.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Red is A, blue is B, the amber number is the middle, and green is outside both.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Put 22 in A and 20 in B. Why can the middle not go below 12?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the two circles in your journal and write the count in each of the four parts.

widgets.title: Checking every case
widgets.challengePrompt: On paper, make a table with four rows: in A and in B, in A only, in B only, in neither. Use it to check that outside A ∪ B means outside A and outside B.
widgets.cutaway: Only the last row is outside A ∪ B. It is also the only row outside A and outside B. So (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′.
widgets.idealised: The rule: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the four rows: in both, in A only, in B only, in neither.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Tick the rows that are inside A ∪ B. Three are, and one is not.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The row outside A ∪ B is the row that is outside A and outside B.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Now tick the rows outside A ∩ B. Which description picks the same three rows?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Copy the table into your journal and mark the rows for each side of the law.

widgets.title: Hunting for a counterexample
widgets.challengePrompt: Test the claim "if a number is odd, it is a multiple of 3" on the numbers 1 to 15. Find every number that breaks it.
widgets.cutaway: 1, 5, 7, 11 and 13 are odd and not multiples of 3. Any one of them breaks the claim.
widgets.idealised: One counterexample is enough to show a claim is false.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the odd numbers from 1 to 15.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Cross out each one that is a multiple of 3. Five numbers are left.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Each number left is odd and not a multiple of 3, so each one is a counterexample.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Now test "if a number is a multiple of 6, it is even". Can you break it?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: In your journal, draw the odd numbers and the multiples of 3 as two circles. Put 5 where it belongs.

widgets.title: Turning round on the number line
widgets.challengePrompt: Predict where the arrow points after 0, 1 and 2 turns. Then set the turns and check.
widgets.cutaway: Each × (−1) turns the arrow to face the other way. Its length stays the same. Two turns bring it back, so (−1) × (−1) = +1.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the turns to 1. The arrow faces the negative numbers.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Set the turns to 2. The arrow faces forward again, the same length as before.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: The green arrow faces the positive numbers. The red arrow faces the negative numbers.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: On paper, try 3 turns and then 4. Odd counts face backward. Even counts face forward.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch the number line and the two turns in your journal.

widgets.title: What two numbers share
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the two numbers to 24 and 36. Predict the HCF and the LCM, then read the bars.
widgets.cutaway: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. The shared primes give the HCF, 12. Every prime either number needs gives the LCM, 72.
widgets.idealised: The check: HCF × LCM = 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the first number to 24 and the second to 36.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The blue bar shows the HCF, 12. The amber bar shows the LCM, 72.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Blue is what the two numbers share. Amber is the smallest number both divide into.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set both numbers to 24. The HCF and the LCM are both 24. Can you say why?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the factor trees for 24 and 36 in your journal and circle the shared primes.

widgets.title: The doubling staircase
widgets.challengePrompt: On paper, write 2¹ to 2¹⁰ as a staircase, each step double the one before. Use it to check that 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷ without multiplying it out.
widgets.cutaway: Going up one step multiplies by 2. Going up 3 steps and then 4 more is 7 steps. That is why the indices add.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: 2³ is 8 and 2⁴ is 16. 8 × 16 = 128, which is the 7th step.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 3 steps and then 4 more steps make 7 steps: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Go down instead. 2⁷ ÷ 2⁴ is 4 steps down from the 7th step. Where do you land?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the staircase in your journal and mark the jump from 2³ to 2⁷.

widgets.title: Lining up the repeating digits
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the repeating digits to 36. Predict what is left when the blue row is taken from the red row. Then read the green box.
widgets.cutaway: The red row is 100 lots of 0.3636… and the blue row is 1 lot. Their digits after the point match, so they cancel. 99 lots are left, and they make 36.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the repeating digits to 36. The red row shows 36.3636… and the blue row shows 0.3636…

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: After the decimal point the two rows are identical. Taking one from the other leaves exactly 36.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the colours
watchSteps.caption: Red is 100 lots of the number. Blue is 1 lot. Green is the 99 lots left over.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the repeating digits to 18. The green box gives 18/99, which is 2/11. Divide 2 by 11 on paper to check.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write the three rows for 0.3636… in your journal, with the matching digits lined up.

widgets.title: How many pieces fit?
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the whole number to 4 and the bottom of the fraction to 3. Predict how many pieces of 2/3 fit into 4. Then read the amber line.
widgets.cutaway: 4 wholes cut into thirds make 12 thirds. Each piece uses 2 of them, so 6 pieces fit. That is 4 × 3 ÷ 2, which is 4 × 3/2.

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the whole number to 4 and the bottom of the fraction to 3.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The amber line counts the pieces. 6 pieces of 2/3 fit into 4.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Multiplying by 3 counts the thirds. Dividing by 2 groups them. Together that is × 3/2.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Keep the whole number at 4 and set the bottom to 6. The pieces are smaller, so more fit. How many?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw 4 bars cut into thirds in your journal and circle the groups of 2.

widgets.title: Sharing in a ratio
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the parts for A to 2 and the parts for B to 6. Every part is worth ₹40. Predict how much A and B each get. Then read the two bars.
widgets.cutaway: Every box is 1 part and holds ₹40. A has 2 boxes and B has 6, so A gets ₹80 and B gets ₹240. Together that is 8 parts, which is ₹320.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 1 part = total ÷ number of parts

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the parts for A to 3 and the parts for B to 5.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Every box is the same size and holds ₹40. A has 3 boxes and B has 5.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: There are 3 + 5 = 8 parts and ₹320 in all. ₹320 ÷ 8 = ₹40 for one part.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set A to 6 and B to 2. The total is still ₹320. Who gets more now, and how much?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the two bars for 3 : 5 in your journal and write ₹40 in every box.

widgets.title: Adding or multiplying, for 20 years
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the interest rate to 10%. Predict what ₹1,000 becomes in 20 years with simple interest. Then guess the compound total, and read the amber lines.
widgets.cutaway: Simple interest adds the same ₹100 every year, so 20 years add ₹2,000. Compound interest multiplies by 1.1 every year. Twenty multiplications turn ₹1,000 into ₹6,727.
widgets.idealised: The rule: multiply by the same number once for each year

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the interest rate to 8%. The amber lines show ₹2,600 with simple interest and ₹4,661 with compound.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Compound interest gives ₹2,061 more, from the same ₹1,000 and the same rate.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Simple interest adds 20 lots of ₹80. Compound interest multiplies by 1.08 twenty times.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the rate to 12%. The rule of 72 says the money doubles every 6 years. Is the compound total more than ₹8,000?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Copy the first three years at 8% into your journal: ₹1,080, ₹1,166.40 and ₹1,259.71.

widgets.title: Two brackets as a rectangle
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the side to 5, the first number to 2 and the second number to 3. Predict the area of each of the four pieces. Then read the rectangle.
widgets.cutaway: The red square is 5 by 5, so it holds 25. The blue strips hold 2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 5 = 15. The amber corner holds 2 × 3 = 6. Together that is 56, and 7 × 8 = 56.
widgets.idealised: The rule: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the side to 4, the first number to 3 and the second number to 2.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red square is x², the blue strips are 3x and 2x, and the amber corner is 6.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 3x and 2x are like terms, so they join to make 5x. The green line reads x² + 5x + 6.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set both numbers to 3. The two strips are the same size now. What is (x + 3)² multiplied out?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the rectangle for (x + 2)(x + 1) in your journal and write the area in each piece.

widgets.title: A square with a corner cut away
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the side to 6 and the first number to 2. Predict 6² − 2² before you read the amber lines.
widgets.cutaway: 6² − 2² = 36 − 4 = 32. The amber lines show the same number as 4 × 8, which is (6 − 2) × (6 + 2).
widgets.idealised: The rule: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the side to 5 and the first number to 3. The amber lines show 5² − 3².

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: 25 − 9 = 16, and the amber lines give 2 × 8, which is also 16.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 2 is the side take away 3, and 8 is the side add 3. So 5² − 3² = (5 − 3)(5 + 3).

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the side to 3 and the first number to 3. Predict the answer, and say why.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a 5 by 5 square, cut a 3 by 3 corner from it, and lay the rest out as a 2 by 8 rectangle.

widgets.title: A balance for an equation
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the bags to 5 and the loose marbles to 4. Predict how many marbles a bag must hold for the right pan to show 19. Then move the last slider.
widgets.cutaway: 5 bags and 4 marbles balance 19 marbles. Take 4 off both pans, and 5 bags balance 15. So each bag holds 3.
widgets.idealised: The rule: ax + b = c gives x = (c − b) ÷ a

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the bags to 2, the loose marbles to 1 and the marbles in a bag to 4.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The right pan shows 9 marbles, and the green line reads 2b + 1 = 9.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Take 1 off both pans: 2b = 8. Share between 2 bags: b = 4, the slider's value.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the loose marbles to 9. What does the right pan show now, and why does b stay 4?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the balance for 3b + 2 = 14 in your journal. Cross out the same marbles on both pans.

widgets.title: Turning a formula round
widgets.challengePrompt: The taxi formula is C = 50 + 12d. Predict the distance for a fare of ₹110 before you work it out.
widgets.cutaway: Undo the steps in reverse order. 110 − 50 = 60, and 60 ÷ 12 = 5, so the ride was 5 km.
widgets.idealised: The rule: C = 50 + 12d gives d = (C − 50) ÷ 12

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the taxi formula as a chain: d, then × 12, then + 50, then C.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Each arrow has an inverse. Adding 50 is undone by taking 50 away, and × 12 by ÷ 12.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Run the chain backwards from C, and you get d = (C − 50) ÷ 12.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Make r the subject of A = 3r + 7. Then find r when A = 25.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the chain for v = u + at forwards and backwards, and read off t.

widgets.title: Turning an inequality round
widgets.challengePrompt: Mark 2 and 5 on a number line. Predict what happens to their order when you multiply both by −1.
widgets.cutaway: 2 < 5, but −2 > −5. Multiplying by −1 reflects every number across 0, so the order turns round.
widgets.idealised: The rule: if a < b, then −a > −b

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a number line from −6 to 6, and mark 2 and 5.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Multiply each by −1. The points −2 and −5 sit on the other side of 0, the other way round.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: So 2 < 5 becomes −2 > −5. Dividing by a negative number turns the order round too.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Solve −3x < 12. Which way does the sign point once you divide by −3?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw x ≥ −1 and x < 4 on one number line, with a filled dot and an open circle.

widgets.title: Two staircases make a rectangle
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the terms to 6, the first term to 1 and the common difference to 1. Predict 1 + 2 + … + 6 before you read the amber line.
widgets.cutaway: The red staircase 1 to 6 and its blue copy turned upside down make a rectangle 6 wide and 7 high. That is 42 squares, so one staircase is 21.
widgets.idealised: The rule: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1) ÷ 2

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the terms to 4, the first term to 1 and the common difference to 1.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Every column, red and blue together, is 5 high.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The rectangle is 4 × 5 = 20, and half of it is 10, which is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the first term to 3 and the common difference to 2. Are the columns still all the same height?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the two staircases for 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 in your journal and find the sum.

widgets.title: Finding the rule from the gaps
widgets.challengePrompt: Write down 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. Predict whether its first differences or its second differences are equal.
widgets.cutaway: The first differences are 4, 6, 8 and 10. The second differences are all 2, so the nth term starts with n².
widgets.idealised: The rule: equal first differences d give dn + c, and equal second differences 2a give an² + …

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Write the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and the gaps under it.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The gaps are all 4, so the nth term starts with 4n.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 4n gives 4, 8, 12, so take 1 away: the nth term is 4n − 1.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Try 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. The first gaps change, so find the gaps of the gaps.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the tile squares for 1, 4 and 9, and colour each new L-shaped border.

widgets.title: Rise over run stays the same
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the gradient to 3 and where the line crosses the y-axis to −2. Predict where it crosses the x-axis before you read the amber line.
widgets.cutaway: y = 3x − 2 crosses the y-axis at (0, −2). Setting y = 0 gives 3x = 2, so it crosses the x-axis at x = 2 ÷ 3.
widgets.idealised: The rule: y = mx + c, with gradient m = change in y ÷ change in x

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the gradient to 1, where the line crosses the y-axis to 0 and the step across to 1.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Change the step across to 3. The rise becomes 3 too, so the gradient is still 1.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Set the gradient to −1. The line now falls 1 for every 1 across.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the gradient to 0. Where does the flat line cross the x-axis?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 on the same axes in your journal. Do they meet?

widgets.title: Reading a journey
widgets.challengePrompt: Kym rides 12 km in 1 hour, rests for 1 hour, then rides home in 2 hours. Predict which part of the line is steepest.
widgets.cutaway: The ride out climbs 12 in 1 hour, so its gradient is 12. The ride home falls 12 in 2 hours, a gradient of −6.
widgets.idealised: The rule: on a distance-time graph, speed = distance ÷ time = the gradient

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Mark the points (0, 0), (1, 12), (2, 12) and (4, 0), and join them.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The flat part is the rest stop. Time passes, but the distance does not change.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The first part rises 12 in 1 hour, which is a speed of 12 km an hour.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: If the ride home took 3 hours, would its line be steeper or less steep?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the line of your own trip to school and back, and find each speed.

widgets.title: Copying the angles across
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the angle at A to 30° and the angle at B to 65°. Predict the angle at C before you read the first line of text.
widgets.cutaway: The green line through C is parallel to AB. The red and blue copies at C are alternate angles, so the three angles at C fill a straight line.
widgets.idealised: The rule: the angles of a triangle add to 180°

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the angle at A to 50° and the angle at B to 60°.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red copy at C sits in a Z with the angle at A, so the two are equal.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The red, grey and blue angles at C fill the green line: 50° + 70° + 60° = 180°.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set both sliders to 65°. How small does the grey angle at C get?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a triangle in your journal with a line through one corner, parallel to the opposite side.

widgets.title: The angle outside the triangle
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the angle at A to 45° and the angle at B to 55°. Predict the amber angle outside B before you read it.
widgets.cutaway: The amber angle and the angle at B share a straight line, so the amber angle is 180° − 55° = 125°. That equals 45° + 80°, the angles at A and C.
widgets.idealised: The rule: an exterior angle of a triangle = the sum of the angles at the other two corners

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the angle at A to 40° and the angle at B to 70°.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The amber angle is 110°, and the angles at A and C are 40° and 70°.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 40° + 70° = 110°, so the exterior angle equals the two angles away from it.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set the sides of the shape to 8. How many triangles does the text say it cuts into?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a triangle, carry one side on with a ruler, and measure the angle outside.

widgets.title: Two arcs and a straight line
widgets.challengePrompt: Move the compass slider to its smallest setting. Predict whether the two arcs still cross, then look.
widgets.cutaway: Each crossing is one compass opening from A and the same opening from B. So the four lines from A and B to the crossings are equal, and together they make a rhombus.
widgets.idealised: The rule: every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is as far from A as from B

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Move the compass slider and watch the two arcs from A and B.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red line through the crossings meets AB at its midpoint, at a right angle.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Each crossing is as far from A as from B, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Open the compasses as wide as they go. Does the red line move?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a line in your journal and bisect it with compasses, keeping the arcs.

widgets.title: Bearings there and back
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the bearing from A to 065°. Predict the back bearing from B before you read it.
widgets.cutaway: The north arrows at A and B are parallel, so the way back points the exact opposite way. The angles at the path are co-interior angles, 65° + 115° = 180°, and the back bearing is 245°.
widgets.idealised: The rule: back bearing = bearing + 180°, or bearing − 180° when the bearing is over 180°

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Move the bearing slider slowly from 25° up to 160°.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The back bearing is always 180° more than the bearing.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 065° + 180° = 245°, read along one path in the two directions.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: On paper, start from 245°. It is over 180°, so take 180° away. Where do you land?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write both bearings in your journal, each with three figures.

widgets.title: Folding a cube from its net
widgets.challengePrompt: Move the fold slider from flat to closed. Predict how many vertices the closed cube has before you count them.
widgets.cutaway: Folding joins edges and corners together, but never adds or removes a face. The cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces, and 8 − 12 + 6 = 2.
widgets.idealised: The rule: Euler's formula, V − E + F = 2, for a solid with flat faces and no holes

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the fold slider to 0, so the net of the cube lies flat.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Slide it to 1. Six squares close up into a cube with 8 vertices.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Count 12 edges and 6 faces: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: On paper, count a pyramid on a square: 5 − 8 + 5. Is it 2 again?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a different cube net in your journal, then check that it folds.

widgets.title: A circle laid out as a strip
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the unfold slider to 0, so you see the whole circle. Predict the length and height of the strip before you slide it to 1.
widgets.cutaway: Half the slices have their curved edges along the bottom, half the circumference, πr. Each slice is one radius tall, so the strip covers πr × r = πr².
widgets.idealised: The rule: the area of a circle is πr²

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Move the unfold slider slowly from 0 to 1.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The slices sit top to tail, and the strip looks like a rectangle.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The strip is πr long and r tall, so its area is πr².

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Make the radius bigger. Does the strip get longer, taller, or both?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a circle cut into 8 slices in your journal, and lay them top to tail.

widgets.title: Two trapeziums make a parallelogram
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the top side a to 3 and the bottom side b to 6. Predict how long the parallelogram made of two copies will be.
widgets.cutaway: Turn a copy of the trapezium over and put it beside the first. Together they make a parallelogram a + b long, so one trapezium is half of (a + b) × h.
widgets.idealised: The rule: the area of a trapezium is ½(a + b) × h

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Move the top side slider and the bottom side slider.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The two copies always fit together into a parallelogram.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: With a = 3 and b = 6, the parallelogram is 9 long, so one trapezium is half of 9 × h.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Make a equal to b. What shape is the trapezium now?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a trapezium in your journal, and a second copy turned over beside it.

widgets.title: A whole grid moved at once
widgets.challengePrompt: Open the page called Shear and rotation. Before you move anything, predict whether the square's area will change.
widgets.cutaway: A shear slides each row of the grid sideways, like pushing a pile of cards. The square leans over, but its bottom and its height stay 1, so its area stays 1.
widgets.idealised: Beyond this chapter: a whole grid can be slid, turned or leaned in one move

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Open the page called Shear and rotation, and watch the grid.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The square leans, but its bottom and height stay 1, so its area stays 1.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Find the move on the page that turns the grid without stretching it.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a square on squared paper, then the same square slid, flipped and turned.

widgets.title: Areas under a stretch
widgets.challengePrompt: Open the page called The determinant is area. Predict whether the stretched square covers more or less than 1 square.
widgets.cutaway: Every small square of the grid is stretched by the same amount. So the area of every shape on the grid is multiplied by one number.
widgets.idealised: The rule: an enlargement with scale factor k multiplies every area by k²

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Open the page called The determinant is area.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Every small square inside the big one grows by the same amount.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The area grows from 1 to 1.625, the same number for every shape on the grid.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: For an enlargement with scale factor 2, predict what number the area is multiplied by.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a 1 cm square and its enlargement with scale factor 3, and count the squares inside.

widgets.title: A point that goes round
widgets.challengePrompt: Turn the point round the circle. Before you start, predict the angle where its height is greatest.
widgets.cutaway: The point sits on a circle of radius 1. Its height above the centre is sin θ, and its distance across is cos θ.
widgets.idealised: The rule: the point at angle θ on the unit circle is (cos θ, sin θ)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Turn the point slowly from 0° round to 90°.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The height grows from 0 to 1, and the distance across shrinks from 1 to 0.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Height is sin θ and distance across is cos θ, because the radius is 1.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Turn past 90°. Predict which of the two becomes negative first.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a circle of radius 10 cm and mark the points at 30°, 45° and 60°.

widgets.title: Three squares on one triangle
widgets.challengePrompt: Look at the triangle under the point on the circle. Predict what the squares on its two shorter sides add up to.
widgets.cutaway: The triangle under the point has a hypotenuse of 1, the radius. Its shorter sides are sin θ and cos θ, so their squares add to 1² = 1.
widgets.idealised: The rule: a² + b² = c², so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Move the point and watch the three squares change size.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The two small squares trade area, but the big square on the radius stays the same.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The square on the radius is 1 × 1 = 1, so the two small squares add to 1.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Find the angle where the two small squares are equal. Predict it first.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the 3, 4, 5 triangle with a square on each side, and count the small squares.

widgets.title: Opening a hinge
widgets.challengePrompt: Open the angle between two sides from 60° to 90° and then to 120°. Predict whether the third side grows or shrinks.
widgets.cutaway: Two sides are hinged at angle C. Below 90° the far side is shorter than Pythagoras' theorem gives, and above 90° it is longer.
widgets.idealised: The rule: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Open the hinge slowly and watch the third side.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: At 90° the third side is what Pythagoras' theorem gives.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: cos 90° = 0, so the part taken away is 0 at a right angle.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Past 90°, cos C is negative. Predict what that does to c².

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw sides of 5 cm and 8 cm at 60°, and measure the third side. It is 7 cm.

widgets.title: Sample size and the error bar
widgets.challengePrompt: Move the sample size from 4 to 16 and then to 64. Predict what happens to the width of the red error bar each time.
widgets.cutaway: High and low readings in a random sample partly cancel out. The standard error is σ ÷ √n, so multiplying the sample size by 4 halves the error bar.
widgets.idealised: The rule: standard error = σ ÷ √n

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Keep the spread σ at 12 and set the sample size n to 4.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: At n = 4, the standard error is 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Slide n to 16: √16 = 4, and the standard error drops to 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Slide n to 64 and check that 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write down the standard error for n = 4, 16 and 64 in your notebook.

widgets.title: Wald's returning planes
widgets.challengePrompt: Look at where the returning planes were hit. Decide whether the armour belongs on the wings with many holes or the engine with none.
widgets.cutaway: You only see the planes that made it back. Holes on the wings show where a plane can take a hit and still fly home; the clean engine marks where a hit is fatal.
widgets.idealised: The rule: ask who is missing from the sample before you trust the count

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Look at the blue plane outline on the right of the figure.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The returning planes have hits on the fuselage and wings, not on the engine.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Planes hit in the engine crashed, so survivorship bias hid them from the count.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Think of a phone survey or a product review where the unhappy people dropped out early.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch the plane and label the missing engine hits as the unseen dropouts.

widgets.title: Histogram bars where area is the count
widgets.challengePrompt: Change the width of the third group from 10 minutes to 30 minutes while keeping its count at 30. Predict the bar height at width 10 and at width 30.
widgets.cutaway: The count in the third group stays 30. When the class width grows from 10 to 30, the frequency density drops from 3 to 1 so the rectangle's area stays 30.
widgets.idealised: The rule: frequency density = count ÷ class width, and bar area = count

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the third group's width to 15 minutes and its count to 30.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red bar's height is 30 ÷ 15 = 2.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Slide the width to 30 minutes: the height drops to 30 ÷ 30 = 1.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Keep width at 25 and slide the count to 50. Check that height becomes 2.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch two bars of widths 10 and 20 that both hold a count of 20.

widgets.title: Balancing at the mean and measuring spread
widgets.challengePrompt: Look at five points balanced at 8. Predict what happens to the standard deviation if every point moves 2 units further from 8.
widgets.cutaway: The mean is the balance point where positive and negative gaps cancel to 0. Squaring the gaps, averaging them and taking the square root gives the standard deviation σ.
widgets.idealised: The rule: σ = √( Σ(x − mean)² ÷ n )

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Start with the five numbers 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 around the mean 8.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Their gaps from 8 are −4, −2, 0, 2 and 4, which add to 0.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Their squares 16, 4, 0, 4 and 16 add to 40, giving variance 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Take the square root: √8 is about 2.83, the typical distance from 8.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a number line from 2 to 14, mark the pivot at 8, and label σ ≈ 2.83 on each side.

widgets.title: The pegboard and Pascal's path counts
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the rows to 6 and step the slot k from 0 across to 6. Predict which slot has the tallest bar when the bounce chance is 50%.
widgets.cutaway: At each peg a ball goes left or right. Slot k collects all paths with k right bounces, and there are ⁿCₖ such paths.
widgets.idealised: The rule: slot k has ⁿCₖ = n! ÷ (k!(n − k)!) paths

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set rows n to 6, slot k to 3, and bounce chance p to 50%.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red middle bar at k = 3 has 20 paths, the tallest on the board.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Slide p to 70% and watch the peak shift toward the right-hand slots.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write out row 4 of path counts (1, 4, 6, 4, 1) and check they add to 16.

widgets.title: Tree branches and counting choices
widgets.challengePrompt: Follow a two-step tree with and without replacement. Predict whether the second-step denominator stays the same or drops by 1.
widgets.cutaway: Along a single path you multiply the fractions on each branch. When order does not matter in a group pick, divide the ordered count by r!.
widgets.idealised: The rule: multiply along branches; divide by r! when order does not matter

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Trace the top path for two red marbles drawn from 5 red and 3 blue without replacement.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The first branch is 5/8 and the second is 4/7.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Multiply along the path: 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Compare with replacement, where the second branch stays 5/8.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the four branches for two picks from 5 red and 3 blue and check the four products add to 1.

widgets.title: The 1,000-person Bayes square
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the condition rate to 2%, sensitivity to 95%, and false-positive rate to 5%. Predict whether the red true-positive box or the amber false-positive box is bigger.
widgets.cutaway: Out of 1,000 people, 20 are sick (19 red true positives) and 980 are healthy (49 amber false positives). The posterior is 19 ÷ (19 + 49) ≈ 27.9%.
widgets.idealised: The rule: P(sick | +) = true positives ÷ (true positives + false positives)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the three sliders to 2%, 95% and 5%.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The red count is 19 and the amber count is 49.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Look at the bar on the far right: 19 ÷ (19 + 49) = 19/68 ≈ 27.9%.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Slide the condition rate up to 10% and watch the red share overtake the amber share.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the 1,000-person tree split into 20 and 980 in your notebook.

widgets.title: Counting 1,000 people through a tree
