widgets.challengePrompt: Follow 1,000 people down the branches: first split by the base rate, then by the test result. Add the two positive tips to find the new denominator.
widgets.cutaway: Replacing decimals with 1,000 whole people turns Bayes' theorem into simple addition: 19 true positives plus 49 false positives make 68 positives in all.
widgets.idealised: The rule: posterior = red tip ÷ (red tip + amber tip)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Start with 1,000 people at the root of the tree.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: 2% sends 20 people down the sick branch and 980 down the healthy branch.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: 95% of 20 gives 19 red; 5% of 980 gives 49 amber; 19 ÷ 68 ≈ 27.9%.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: What if a second independent test is run on those 68 people?

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write the four leaf counts (19, 1, 49, 931) and check they add to 1,000.

widgets.title: Sliding the secant into the tangent
widgets.challengePrompt: Keep x₀ at 1.25 on y = ½x² and shrink the step h from 0.8 down to 0.05. Predict the value that the secant slope approaches.
widgets.cutaway: On y = ½x², the derivative is x. As the step h shrinks toward 0, the secant slope x₀ + ½h approaches the exact tangent slope x₀.
widgets.idealised: The rule: f′(x) = the limit as h → 0 of (f(x + h) − f(x)) ÷ h

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set x₀ to 1.5 and step h to 0.5 in the figure.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The amber secant line cuts across the curve above the red tangent line.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Slide h down to 0.05: the secant slope settles onto the tangent slope 1.5.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Move x₀ to 2.0 and check that the red tangent slope equals 2.0.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch a parabola with a secant line through two points and a tangent line at one point.

widgets.title: Two strips on a growing square
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the square's side x to 3 and grow it by a thin strip h. Count the two long strips of length 3 and see what happens to the tiny corner h².
widgets.cutaway: Growing a square of side x by h adds two strips of area x × h and a corner of area h². Dividing by h leaves 2x + h, which becomes 2x as h shrinks to 0.
widgets.idealised: The rule: d/dx(x²) = 2x, and d/dx(xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set the square side x to 2 and the step h to 0.5.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The new area is two strips of 2 × 0.5 plus a corner of 0.5 × 0.5.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Divide by h: 2(2) + 0.5 = 4.5, which approaches 2(2) = 4 as h → 0.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set x to 3 and check that 2x + h approaches 6.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a square of side x with two border strips of width h and label their areas.

widgets.title: Midpoint strips under a curve
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the upper edge x to 2.0 and the slope k to 1.0, then slide the number of strips N from 4 to 20. Watch the sum of the strips compared with the exact area ½kx².
widgets.cutaway: Each strip has width Δx = x ÷ N and height measured at its midpoint. On a straight line the left and right triangles on top of each strip balance, and on a curve the error vanishes as N grows.
widgets.idealised: The rule: ∫₀ˣ kt dt = ½kx²

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set upper edge x to 2.0, strips N to 4, and slope k to 1.0.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Each of the 4 blue strips has width 2.0 ÷ 4 = 0.5.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The 4 strips add to ½ × 1.0 × 2.0² = 2.0.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Slide x to 3.0 and check that the area grows to ½ × 1.0 × 3.0² = 4.5.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the triangle under y = t from 0 to 2 and split it into 2 midpoint strips.

widgets.title: How area and slope undo each other
widgets.challengePrompt: Compare the area under the line y = t from 0 to x with the height of the parabola F(x) = ½x². Predict the rate at which the area grows when you nudge x right by dx.
widgets.cutaway: Nudging the right edge x by a thin step dx adds one vertical ribbon of width dx and height f(x). So the rate of change of the area with respect to x is the curve's height f(x) itself.
widgets.idealised: The rule: d/dx (∫₀ˣ f(t) dt) = f(x), and ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set x to 2.0 and slope k to 1.0.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The height of the line at x = 2 is 2, and the area from 0 to 2 is ½(2)² = 2.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Differentiate ½x²: the power rule gives ½(2x) = x, the height of the line.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set k to 1.5 and x to 2.0: the area is ½(1.5)(4) = 3.0 and the height is 3.0.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Sketch a curve f(x), shade the area to x, and draw one thin new strip of area f(x) dx at the right edge.

widgets.title: Chaining vectors nose to tail
widgets.challengePrompt: Change the lengths of vectors a and b and the angle between them. Watch the green resultant arrow a + b and the dot product.
widgets.cutaway: Placing the tail of b at the tip of a forms a triangle whose third side is the resultant a + b. At 90°, the two vectors are perpendicular and their dot product is 0.
widgets.idealised: The rule: a + b = (x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂), and a · b = |a||b| cos θ

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set vector a to 3 and vector b to 4, with 90° between them.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: At 90° the dot product is 0 and the resultant length is √(3² + 4²) = 5.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Close the angle to 0°: both arrows line up and the resultant length is 3 + 4 = 7.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Open the angle to 120° and notice that the dot product becomes negative.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw a = (3, 1) and b = (1, 3) nose to tail on squared paper and read off a + b = (4, 4).

widgets.title: Vector proof of the triangle midsegment
widgets.challengePrompt: Follow the path from midpoint M of OA through O to midpoint N of OB. Express MN in terms of a and b and compare it with AB = b − a.
widgets.cutaway: Because OM = ½a and ON = ½b, the vector from M to N is ON − OM = ½b − ½a = ½(b − a) = ½AB. One line of vector algebra proves MN is both parallel to AB and half its length.
widgets.idealised: The rule: MN = ½(b − a) = ½AB

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Label OA as vector a and OB as vector b, so AB = b − a.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: Midpoint M sits at ½a and midpoint N sits at ½b.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: Travel from M to N via O: MN = −½a + ½b = ½(b − a).

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: What if P and Q sit one third of the way along OA and OB? Then PQ = ⅓AB.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw any triangle OAB, mark the midpoints M and N, and label MN = ½(b − a).

widgets.title: Basis columns and the determinant parallelogram
widgets.challengePrompt: Set a = 2, b = 1 and d = 2 in the figure. Compare the area det(A) = ad − bc with the product of the two eigenvalues λ₁ × λ₂.
widgets.cutaway: The red arrow is column 1 and the blue arrow is column 2. They span an amber parallelogram of area ad − bc, which also equals the product of the two eigenvalues λ₁ × λ₂.
widgets.idealised: The rule: det([[a, b], [c, d]]) = ad − bc = λ₁ × λ₂

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set column 1 x (a) to 2, off-diagonal (b) to 1, and column 2 y (d) to 2.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The amber parallelogram has area 2 × 2 − 1 × 1 = 3.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The eigenvalues are λ₁ = 3 and λ₂ = 1, and 3 × 1 = 3 = det(A).

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Set a = 1.5, b = 1.5 and d = 1.5 so both arrows line up: det(A) drops to 0.

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Draw the parallelogram spanned by (2, 1) and (1, 2) inside a 3 × 3 square and check its area is 3.

widgets.title: Stretching along eigenvector axes
widgets.challengePrompt: Set the off-diagonal slider b to 0 so the matrix is [[a, 0], [0, d]]. Predict which two directions are the eigenvectors and what their eigenvalues are.
widgets.cutaway: When b = 0, the red arrow stays on the x-axis with length a and the blue arrow stays on the y-axis with length d. The axes themselves are the eigenvectors, with eigenvalues a and d.
widgets.idealised: The rule: Av = λv along each eigenvector axis

watchSteps.title: 1. Try it
watchSteps.caption: Set a to 2.5, b to 0, and d to 1.5.

watchSteps.title: 2. Notice
watchSteps.caption: The amber shape is a 2.5 by 1.5 rectangle of area 3.75.

watchSteps.title: 3. Match the rule
watchSteps.caption: The eigenvalues are λ₁ = 2.5 and λ₂ = 1.5.

watchSteps.title: 4. Push it further
watchSteps.caption: Slide b to −1.0 and watch the parallelogram shear while det(A) = ad − b².

watchSteps.title: 5. Draw it
watchSteps.caption: Write down a 2×2 matrix that doubles x and triples y, and find its determinant.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 3 · Surface-Area-to-Volume Ratio (6L² vs L³)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why Elephants Have Huge Ears & Cells Stay Microscopic (SA:V Scaling)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: When a cell or animal scales up by factor k, its surface area grows as k² while its volume grows as k³. So SA/V = 6/L drops inversely with size.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: SA = 6L²,   V = L³   ⇒   SA : V = 6 / L
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: If a cubical cell doubles its side length from L = 1 μm to L = 2 μm (k = 2), by what factor does its Surface-Area-to-Volume ratio change?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Surface area multiplies by 2² = 4 and volume by 2³ = 8, so SA:V halves from 6:1 to 3:1.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: KymBio Ch 13 · Mendel's Punnett Squares & Clinical Screening
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Punnett Grids Are 2×2 Area Diagrams & Medical Tests Obey Bayes' Rule
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: A Punnett square for Aa × Aa is the algebraic expansion (0.5A + 0.5a)² = 0.25AA + 0.50Aa + 0.25aa, and genetic carrier screening relies on Bayes' theorem.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: In a cross Aa × Aa, an offspring shows the dominant trait (AA or Aa). What is the conditional probability that it is a carrier (Aa)?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Out of 3 dominant-phenotype boxes (1 AA and 2 Aa), 2 are Aa, so P(Aa | Dominant) = 2/3.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Physics Ch 1 · Motion (Velocity Slope & Displacement Area)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Velocity Is the Derivative of Position; Displacement Is the Area Under v(t)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: On a distance-time graph, gradient Δs/Δt is speed. On a speed-time graph, the area of the trapezium under v(t) is distance travelled s = v₀t + ½at².
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: v(t) = ds/dt,   Δs = ∫ v(t) dt = v₀t + ½at²
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: A train accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s over 8 seconds. Using the trapezium area under v(t), how far does it travel?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Physics Ch 2 · Newton's Laws & Inclined Planes
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Resolving Forces on a Ramp with Unit-Circle Sine & Cosine Shadows
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: A block of weight mg sits on a ramp at angle θ. Gravity splits into mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into the ramp.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: F_parallel = mg sin θ,   F_normal = mg cos θ
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: For a 100 N crate on a 30° ramp, what component of gravity pulls it down the slope?

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Atlas of Chemistry · Balancing Equations as Linear Conservation & Mole Ratios

schoolTextbook.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary Complete Mathematics 8 (Second Edition)

units.title: Integers, powers and roots
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 7–24 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing negative integers
topics.summary: Multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the sign round on the number line. Two negative signs make a positive; one negative and one positive make a negative.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 1.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Squares, cubes, roots and indices
topics.summary: A square number is a whole number multiplied by itself, and a cube number is multiplied by itself three times. In prime factors, a square has even powers and a cube has powers that are multiples of 3.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 1.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Index notation
topics.summary: When multiplying powers of the same base, add the indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. When dividing, subtract the indices: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, and a⁰ = 1.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 1.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Prime factorization to find the HCF and LCM
topics.summary: Break each number into prime factors with a factor tree. The highest common factor (HCF) multiplies the shared primes; the lowest common multiple (LCM) takes each prime the most times it appears.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 1.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.summary: Work out brackets and powers before multiplying and dividing, and add or subtract last. Notice that (−3)² = +9, whereas −3² means −(3 × 3) = −9.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 1.5.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Natural numbers and rational numbers
topics.summary: Whole numbers, negative numbers and fractions are rational numbers, which stop or repeat as decimals. A square root of a non-square whole number, such as √2, is an irrational number.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 1.6.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Expressions
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 25–36 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Expressions, formulae and equations
topics.summary: An expression has no = sign, such as 3x + 2. An equation is true for only some values of x, such as 3x + 2 = 11. An identity is true for every value, such as 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 2.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Expanding brackets
topics.summary: A number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside, signs included: −3(x − 5) = −3x + 15. For two brackets, multiply each term of one by each term of the other, then collect like terms.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 2.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Factorizing expressions
topics.summary: Take the HCF of every term outside a bracket, numbers and letters both: 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Then check that nothing common is left inside. A difference of two squares factorises as (a − b)(a + b).
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 2.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Substitution into expressions
topics.summary: Put each number in a bracket as you substitute it. When x = −4, x² is (−4)² = 16, but −x² is −16. Work out powers before you multiply.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 2.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Shapes and mathematical drawings
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 37–58 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Quadrilaterals
topics.summary: A quadrilateral has four sides, and its angles add to 360°. A rhombus and a kite have diagonals that cross at right angles, and a rectangle has diagonals of equal length.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 3.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: 3D shapes
topics.summary: A net of a solid folds up into it, and the plan view and elevations show it from above, the front and the side. For a solid with no holes, Euler's formula says V − E + F = 2.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 3.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Bearings
topics.summary: A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, from 000° to 359°. The back bearing differs by 180°, so 065° gives 245°.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 3.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Constructions
topics.summary: Three sides (SSS), two sides and the angle between them (SAS), or two angles and the side between them (ASA) fix a triangle. Triangles that match in one of these ways are congruent.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 3.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Bisecting angles and lines
topics.summary: The perpendicular bisector of AB is the locus of points equally far from A and B. An angle bisector is the locus of points equally far from the two arms of the angle.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 3.5.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Sampling
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 59–64 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Methods of data collection
topics.summary: Primary data is data you collect yourself by counting, measuring or asking questions. Secondary data comes from a table or record someone else already gathered. A fair questionnaire uses short, neutral questions and non-overlapping answer boxes that cover every possible reply.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 4.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Sampling methods
topics.summary: A random sample gives every member of the population the same chance. A systematic sample picks every kth member from a numbered list, and a stratified sample takes from each group in proportion to its size.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 4.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Area, perimeter and volume
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 65–86 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Circumference of a circle
topics.summary: The circumference of a circle is π times its diameter, C = πd = 2πr, with π about 3.14. A sector with angle θ has θ/360 of the circle's area and of its circumference.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 5.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Areas of parallelograms and trapeziums
topics.summary: A parallelogram's area is base × height. A trapezium's area is ½(a + b) × h. In both, the height is measured at a right angle to the base.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 5.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Volume of a triangular prism
topics.summary: The volume of a prism is the area of its cross-section × its length. A triangular prism with a 12 cm² triangle at each end and a length of 20 cm holds 240 cm³.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 5.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Surface area of prisms and pyramids
topics.summary: The surface area of a solid adds up the areas of all its faces. Draw its net, find the area of each face, and add them.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 5.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Imperial units
topics.summary: Some lengths, weights and amounts are still given in older units. 5 miles is about 8 km, 1 inch is about 2.5 cm, 1 kg is about 2.2 pounds, and 1 litre is about 1.76 pints.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 5.5.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Fractions and decimals
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 87–105 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals
topics.summary: Multiply decimals as whole numbers, then count the decimal places back in. To divide by a decimal, first multiply both numbers by 10 or 100 so you divide by a whole number.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 6.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Significant figures
topics.summary: Significant figures are counted from the first digit that is not zero. Round once, at the end of a calculation.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 6.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Recurring decimals
topics.summary: A fraction in simplest form gives a decimal that stops only when its denominator is built from 2s and 5s. Otherwise the digits repeat. To turn a recurring decimal into a fraction, multiply so the repeating tails line up, then subtract.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 6.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Subtracting mixed numbers
topics.summary: Write both mixed numbers as improper fractions. Give them a common denominator, then subtract the numerators.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 6.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
topics.summary: To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 6.5.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Equations, formulae and inequalities
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 106–125 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Deriving formulae
topics.summary: Turn words or a diagram into a formula. Give each quantity a letter and a unit. A rectangle L cm long and w cm wide has perimeter P = 2(L + w).
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 7.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Deriving and solving equations
topics.summary: Do the same to both sides. Expand any brackets, and clear a fraction by multiplying both sides by its bottom number. Gather the letter terms on one side, then check the answer in the first equation.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 7.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Changing the subject of a formula
topics.summary: To change the subject, undo the steps in reverse order on both sides. If the new subject appears twice, gather both terms on one side and factorise to take it out.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 7.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Inequalities
topics.summary: Solve an inequality like an equation. On a number line, < and > get an open circle, and ≤ and ≥ a filled dot. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the sign round.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 7.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Geometry
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 126–137 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Exterior angle of a triangle
topics.summary: An exterior angle of a triangle lies between one side carried on and the next side. It equals the sum of the angles at the other two corners, so angles of 50° and 70° give an exterior angle of 120°.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 8.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Angles in parallel lines and intersecting lines
topics.summary: Where two lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal. When a transversal cuts parallel lines, corresponding angles (F) and alternate angles (Z) are equal, and co-interior angles (C) add to 180°.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 8.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Midpoint of a line segment
topics.summary: The midpoint of a line segment averages the coordinates of its ends. The midpoint of (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is ((x₁ + x₂) ÷ 2, (y₁ + y₂) ÷ 2).
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 8.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Decimals, percentages and fractions
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 138–148 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Multiplying by decimals
topics.summary: Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount smaller. 0.4 of something is less than all of it.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 9.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Dividing by decimals
topics.summary: Dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes a positive amount bigger. Scale both numbers up until you divide by a whole number: 7 ÷ 0.25 is 700 ÷ 25.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 9.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Percentage increase and decrease
topics.summary: A percentage change is one multiplication. A 15% rise is × 1.15 and a 15% fall is × 0.85. To go back to the old amount, divide by the multiplier. Changes in a row multiply.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 9.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Simplifying calculations with fractions and decimals
topics.summary: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways to write one number: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Pick the form that makes the sum shortest.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 9.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Presenting data and interpreting results
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 149–172 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Time series graphs
topics.summary: A time series graph plots measurements in time order with time on the horizontal axis. A moving average averages fixed-length windows to smooth regular seasonal swings and show the trend.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 10.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Stem-and-leaf diagrams
topics.summary: A stem-and-leaf diagram splits each number into a leading stem and a trailing leaf written in order, with a key. Back-to-back diagrams compare two groups on the same stems.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 10.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Histograms
topics.summary: A histogram shows continuous grouped data with no gaps between bars. When class widths differ, bar height is frequency density = count ÷ class width, so bar area equals the count.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 10.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Interpreting and comparing data and diagrams
topics.summary: To compare two distributions fairly, compare one measure of middle (mean or median) and one measure of spread (interquartile range or standard deviation).
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 10.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Sequences
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 173–183 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Rules of sequences
topics.summary: A term-to-term rule makes each term from the one before, like add 4 or multiply by 2. Equal gaps make an arithmetic sequence. Multiplying by the same number each time makes a geometric sequence.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 11.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: The nth term
topics.summary: The nth term gives any term from its position n. For equal gaps d it is dn + c. Equal second differences give a quadratic sequence with an n². To add an arithmetic sequence, multiply the number of terms by the first plus the last, then halve.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 11.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Ratio and proportion
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 184–193 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Units of measurement
topics.summary: A length in metres is 100 times as many centimetres. An area has two lengths, so multiply by 100 twice: 1 m² = 10,000 cm². A volume has three, so 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 12.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Simplifying ratio
topics.summary: Put both amounts in the same unit first. Then divide every part of the ratio by a common factor until no more will go.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 12.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Sharing in a given ratio
topics.summary: Add the parts, find what one part is worth, then multiply for each share. If you are told a difference and not the total, match it to the difference in parts.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 12.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Proportion
topics.summary: In direct proportion, both amounts are multiplied by the same number. In inverse proportion, one is multiplied and the other is divided, so multiplying them together always gives the same answer.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 12.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Transformations
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 194–211 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Translations
topics.summary: A translation slides a shape without turning it. It is written as a column vector, the step across on top and the step up below. The shape's size and the way it faces stay the same.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 13.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Reflections
topics.summary: A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. Each point and its image are the same distance from the mirror, measured at a right angle. Reflecting in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 13.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Rotations
topics.summary: A rotation turns a shape about a centre of rotation. To describe one, give the centre, the angle, and clockwise or anticlockwise.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 13.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Symmetry
topics.summary: A line of symmetry flips a shape onto itself. The order of rotational symmetry counts how many times a shape fits onto itself in one full turn. A cube can be cut into two mirror halves in 9 ways.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 13.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Enlargements
topics.summary: An enlargement multiplies every distance from the centre of enlargement by the scale factor k. Lengths are multiplied by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 13.5.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Functions and graphs
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 212–229 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Functions
topics.summary: A function machine follows a rule step by step, like f(x) = 2x + 3. Its inverse undoes the steps in reverse order, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3) ÷ 2.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 14.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Linear graphs
topics.summary: The line y = mx + c has gradient m, the change in y divided by the change in x, and crosses the y-axis at (0, c). Parallel lines have the same gradient. Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1. Two lines meet at the point that fits both equations.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 14.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Real-life graphs
topics.summary: A real-life graph shows a steady rate as a straight line. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, and a flat part means standing still.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 14.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: Probability
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 230–248 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: The idea of probability
topics.summary: Probability measures how likely an outcome is on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When outcomes cannot happen together they are mutually exclusive, their probabilities add up, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 15.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Experimental probability
topics.summary: Experimental probability is successes ÷ trials. As you run more trials, the experimental probability settles closer to the theoretical probability.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 15.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Theoretical probability
topics.summary: When all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely, P(A) = wanted outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Factorials, permutations and combinations count large sample spaces without listing every item.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 15.3.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Combined events
topics.summary: Two-way sample-space grids and tree diagrams organise combined events. Multiply along branches to find the probability of a path, and add separate paths at the end.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 15.4.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

units.title: BONUS CHAPTER: Vectors
units.scienceInContext: OUP Complete Mathematics 8 (2nd Ed.) pp. 249–260 + Built-In 3-Tier Singapore & Checkpoint Companion Workbook.

topics.title: Introduction to vectors
topics.summary: A vector has both magnitude (length) and direction, written as a column vector (x, y). Multiplying by a scalar scales both components, and the magnitude is |v| = √(x² + y²) by Pythagoras' theorem.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 16.1.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

topics.title: Using vectors in geometry
topics.summary: Vectors add nose to tail by the triangle law AB + BC = AC, and AB = OB − OA. Showing one vector is a scalar multiple of another proves they are parallel, or collinear if they share a point.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw a bar model or sketch the geometry before writing the formula for 16.2.
Check units, negative signs, and significant figures at the final step.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) and Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of 72 and 120 using prime factorisation, and verify that HCF × LCM = 72 × 120.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1: Break both into prime factors: 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5.
Step 2: Multiply the primes they share for the HCF: 2³ × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24.
Step 3: Take the highest power of each prime for the LCM: 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.
Step 4: Check: 24 × 360 = 8,640, and 72 × 120 = 8,640.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5, so HCF = ___ and LCM = ___.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: HCF = 24 and LCM = 360 because 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; their overlap is 2³ × 3 = 24 and their union is 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360.

mistakes.name: You mixed up HCF and LCM
mistakes.nextStep: The HCF takes the lower power of each shared prime, and the LCM takes the higher power of every prime.

mistakes.name: You took the LCM as the numbers multiplied together
mistakes.nextStep: The LCM uses each prime once at its highest power, so rebuild it from the two prime factor lists.

stuck.sister: Find the HCF and LCM of 12 and 18 using prime factors.

steps.prompt: Write 12 as a product of prime factors, using powers.

schoolQuestions.prompt: A rare genetic trait occurs in 2% of a population (P(D) = 0.02). A screening test has 95% sensitivity (P(+|D) = 0.95) and a 5% false-positive rate (P(+|¬D) = 0.05). Out of 1,000 people, find the number of True Positives, False Positives, and P(D | +).
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1: Out of 1,000 people, 2% have the trait: 0.02 × 1,000 = 20 people, and 980 do not.
Step 2: True positives = 95% of 20 = 0.95 × 20 = 19 people.
Step 3: False positives = 5% of 980 = 0.05 × 980 = 49 people.
Step 4: Out of 19 + 49 = 68 positive tests, P(D | +) = 19/68 ≈ 27.9%.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Given column vectors a = (3, 4)ᵀ and b = (2, −1)ᵀ, calculate 2a − 3b and find the exact magnitude |a|.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1: Scale each vector: 2a = 2(3, 4) = (6, 8) and 3b = 3(2, −1) = (6, −3).
Step 2: Subtract component by component: 2a − 3b = (6 − 6, 8 − (−3)) = (0, 11).
Step 3: By Pythagoras' theorem, |a| = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

polyaStages.title: 1. Understand the Problem
polyaStages.subtitle: Isolate the unknown, the given data, and the governing condition
prompts: What is the unknown? Can I name it or draw it as a Singapore bar segment?
What are the data and units? Are any quantities hidden in words like 'bisects', 'regular', or 'independent'?
What condition links the data to the unknown? Is it enough to fix the unknown?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: A train passes a 300 m platform in 24 seconds and passes a standing lamp-post in 9 seconds at constant speed. Find the length of the train.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Unknown: Train length L. Data: Lamp-post time = 9 s (covers L only); Platform time = 24 s (covers L + 300 m). Same in both: speed v is constant.

polyaStages.title: 2. Devise a Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Choose a plan: draw a bar model, try a simpler case, work backwards, or look for symmetry
prompts: Can I draw a bar model or add a helper line to the shape?
What happens in a tiny case (n = 1, 2, 3) — does a pattern of differences emerge?
Can I work backwards from the target or use an extreme case (h → 0, θ = 0° or 90°)?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Compare the two journeys of the train on a single Singapore distance bar.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Draw two bars: Bar 1 = [Train L] takes 9 s. Bar 2 = [Train L] + [300 m] takes 24 s. The extra 300 m alone takes 24 − 9 = 15 s.

polyaStages.title: 3. Carry Out the Plan
polyaStages.subtitle: Execute each algebraic or geometric step and check that every step is reversible
prompts: Can I prove that each step follows from the line above it?
Did I keep units and signs consistent across every operation?
Can I see the geometric meaning of the intermediate number?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Compute the train's speed from the 15-second difference and find L.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Speed v = 300 m ÷ 15 s = 20 m/s. Since passing the lamp-post takes 9 s, Train length L = 20 m/s × 9 s = 180 m.

polyaStages.title: 4. Look Back & Generalise
polyaStages.subtitle: Sanity-check dimensions, test a second method, and turn the result into a reusable formula
prompts: Does the answer survive a substitution check in the original problem?
Can I derive the general formula for any platform length P and times t₁, t₂?
Where else can I use this 'subtract the two states to isolate the difference' trick?
polyaStages.exampleProblem: Verify L = 180 m and write the universal formula.
polyaStages.phaseBreakdown: Check: (180 + 300) m ÷ 20 m/s = 480 ÷ 20 = 24 s ✓. General Formula: L = P · t₁ / (t₂ − t₁).

visualMathTips.title: Why minus times minus is plus
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Multiplying by −1 turns you round on the number line.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Two about-turns leave you facing the way you started.

visualMathTips.title: Why (a + b)² is not a² + b²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Draw a square of side a + b. Mark a and b along the top and down the side, and cut it into four pieces.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: There are the corner squares a² and b², and also two strips of area ab. Leave out the 2ab and the square has two gaps.

visualMathTips.title: Why 1 + 2 + … + n is half of n(n + 1)
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Build a staircase of 1, 2, 3, … up to n blocks. Make a copy and turn it upside down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Set the copy on top, and every column reaches n + 1. The two staircases fill a rectangle n by n + 1, so one staircase is half of it.

visualMathTips.title: Why a circle's area is πr²
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Cut a circle into 24 thin slices and lay them top to tail, points up and points down.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: The strip is half the circumference long, πr, and one radius tall, r.

visualMathTips.title: Why sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: On a circle of radius 1, the point at angle θ sits sin θ up and cos θ across from the centre.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Those two lengths are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is 1.

visualMathTips.title: Why a positive result from a 95% accurate test is right only 28% of the time
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: In a square of 1,000 people at a 2% base rate, only 20 people are sick while 980 are healthy.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: A 5% false-alarm rate on 980 healthy people creates 49 false positives, which outnumber the 19 true positives.

visualMathTips.title: Why slope and area undo each other
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Compare the shaded triangle of area under f′(t) = t from 0 to x with the height of the parabola f(x) = ½x².
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Each thin strip of area f′(t) × dt is a tiny step df on the original curve. All the strips add up to f(x) − f(0).

visualMathTips.title: Why det(A) = ad − bc is area
visualMathTips.visualIntuition: Place the parallelogram spanned by (a, c) and (b, d) inside a bounding rectangle of width a + b and height c + d.
visualMathTips.ahaMoment: Taking away four right-angled triangles (total area ac + bd) and two b × c corner rectangles (total area 2bc) from (a + b)(c + d) leaves ad − bc.

You matched the difference to the wrong units
You scaled an area by the length factor
You used direct proportion where it is inverse
You joined the ratios without matching the shared part
You enlarged from the origin, not the centre
You reflected in the wrong mirror line
You turned the wrong way
You undid the steps in the wrong order
You took one over f instead of the inverse
You did not both flip and negate the gradient
You turned the condition round
You divided by the wrong total
You treated the sums as equally likely
You mixed up whether order matters
You forgot the first marble stays out
You combined the vectors the wrong way

footings.skill: Multiply and divide negative numbers
footings.teach: Same signs make a positive and different signs make a negative, so (−3) × (−2) = 6 and 6 ÷ (−3) = −2, and a minus sign stays with its number through every step. Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number turns the sign round: −x < 2 becomes x > −2.

probes.prompt: Work out 2 × 3 − 4 × 5.
Solve −2x < 8.

footings.skill: Undo each step with its inverse
footings.teach: Undo the last step first and do the same to both sides. For x/2 + 3 = 8, take 3 from both sides to get x/2 = 5, then multiply by 2 to get x = 10. An inverse function f⁻¹ makes those undo steps; it is not 1 ÷ f.

probes.prompt: Solve x + 9 = 4.
Solve x/4 − 3 = 2.
f(x) = 2x + 1. Find f⁻¹(9).

footings.skill: Multiply every term inside a bracket
footings.teach: The number outside a bracket multiplies each term inside it: −3(x − 4) = −3x + 12. A squared bracket is two brackets, so (x + 2)² = (x + 2)(x + 2) = x² + 4x + 4, not x² + 4.

probes.prompt: Expand −2(x − 5).
Expand (x + 3)².
Work out 7² − 3², then (7 − 3)².

footings.skill: Find the HCF and LCM, and cancel fully
footings.teach: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both, and the LCM is the smallest number both divide into. For 4 and 10, the HCF is 2 and the LCM is 20, not 4 × 10 = 40. Cancel a fraction by the HCF so nothing common is left, as in 10/15 = 2/3.

probes.prompt: Find the LCM of 6 and 8.
Find the HCF of 18 and 24.
Write 18/24 in its simplest form.

footings.skill: Square a number and undo it with a square root
footings.teach: Squaring multiplies a number by itself, so 5² = 5 × 5 = 25, not 10, and a square root undoes it: √25 = 5. In a right-angled triangle, square the two shorter sides, add, then take the square root: 3² + 4² = 25, so the longest side is 5.

probes.prompt: Work out 6².
x² = 64 and x is positive. Find x.
A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the longest side.

footings.skill: Use a common denominator and improper fractions
footings.teach: Add or subtract fractions only once they share a denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6, never 2/5. Turn a mixed number into an improper fraction first, so 1 1/2 is 3/2.

probes.prompt: Work out 1/3 + 1/4.
Work out 2 1/3 − 1 2/3.
Work out 2 1/2 × 1 1/5.

footings.skill: Round to decimal places and significant figures
footings.teach: Look at the digit after the last one you keep and round up if it is 5 or more, so 2.367 to 2 decimal places is 2.37, not 2.36. Significant figures start at the first digit that is not zero: 0.005281 to 2 significant figures is 0.0053.

probes.prompt: Round 4.2861 to 2 decimal places.
Round 0.07368 to 2 significant figures.
Round 52,718 to 2 significant figures.

footings.skill: Multiply and divide by 10, 100 and decimals
footings.teach: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left, so 0.47 × 100 = 47, and a recurring decimal never stops, so 10 × 0.333… take away 0.333… is exactly 3. To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 until it is whole: 12 ÷ 0.3 = 120 ÷ 3 = 40.

probes.prompt: Work out 0.36 × 100.
Work out 36 ÷ 0.4.
x = 0.555…, where the fives go on for ever. Work out 10x − x.

footings.skill: Choose multiply or divide, and which way round
footings.teach: Ask what one of something is worth: if 4 pens cost £6, one pen costs 6 ÷ 4 = £1.50, and the amount you share out goes first. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a bigger answer, so 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4.

probes.prompt: A car goes 75 km on 6 litres of fuel. How far does it go on 1 litre?
How many 0.25 kg bags can be filled from 3 kg of rice?
A 1.5 m ribbon is cut into pieces 0.3 m long. How many pieces are there?

footings.skill: Work out what one part is worth
footings.teach: Find one part first: to share 45 in the ratio 4 : 5, there are 9 parts, so one part is 5 and the shares are 20 and 25. If more workers do the same job, it takes less time: 2 workers taking 6 hours means 1 worker takes 12 hours.

probes.prompt: Share 60 in the ratio 2 : 3.
4 workers paint a fence in 6 days. How long would 8 workers take at the same rate?
Two amounts are in the ratio 2 : 5. The larger is 15 more than the smaller. What is the smaller amount?

footings.skill: Use a multiplier for a percentage change
footings.teach: A percentage change is one multiplication: a 30% decrease is × 0.7 and a 5% increase is × 1.05. Two changes multiply, so up 40% then down 40% is × 1.4 × 0.6 = × 0.84, and to undo a change you divide by its multiplier.

probes.prompt: What do you multiply by to decrease an amount by 15%?
A price rises by 10%, then rises by 10% again. What single multiplier does the same?
After a 20% increase, a coat costs £60. What did it cost before the increase?

footings.skill: Convert units, and square the factor for areas
footings.teach: Change every length to the same unit before you calculate: 1 m = 100 cm, so 3.2 m = 320 cm. An area scales by the square of the length factor, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm², and doubling every length makes an area 4 times as big.

probes.prompt: Write 2.5 m in centimetres.
How many cm² are there in 3 m²?
A shape has area 5 cm². It is enlarged by scale factor 3. What is its new area?

footings.skill: Use the right lengths in area and perimeter
footings.teach: A triangle's area is half of base × perpendicular height, so base 6 cm and height 4 cm give 12 cm², and a slanted side is never the height. Use the radius in πr², and add every edge for a perimeter: a quarter circle of radius 2 cm has perimeter π + 4.

probes.prompt: A triangle has base 12 cm, a slanted side 10 cm and perpendicular height 8 cm. Find its area.
A semicircle has diameter 10 cm. Find its perimeter, using π = 3.14.
A circle has diameter 12 cm. Find its area in terms of π.

footings.skill: Use angle facts for parallel lines, polygons and bearings
footings.teach: Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. An exterior angle of a polygon is 180° take away the interior angle, so an interior angle of 108° has exterior angle 72°. A back-bearing is the bearing plus 180°, or minus 180° if that passes 360°: the back-bearing of 050° is 230°.

probes.prompt: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 115°. Find the other.
Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 150°. What is each exterior angle?
The bearing of B from A is 120°. What is the bearing of A from B?

footings.skill: Find a midpoint and a gradient from coordinates
footings.teach: The midpoint averages the x-coordinates and then the y-coordinates, keeping x first: the midpoint of (1, 2) and (5, 10) is (3, 6). Gradient is change in y ÷ change in x, and a perpendicular gradient flips it and changes its sign, so 2/3 becomes −3/2.

probes.prompt: Find the midpoint of (2, 3) and (8, 11).
Find the gradient of the line through (2, 1) and (5, 13).
A line has gradient 3. What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to it?

footings.skill: Reflect, rotate and enlarge a point
footings.teach: Check the mirror line or centre before you move. Reflecting (3, 4) in the y-axis gives (−3, 4), and a 90° turn clockwise about the origin takes (x, y) to (y, −x). To enlarge about a centre, multiply the step from the centre to the point, then add it back on: (3, 2) from centre (1, 1) by scale factor 3 is (7, 4).

probes.prompt: Reflect the point (2, 5) in the x-axis.
Rotate the point (3, 1) through 90° clockwise about the origin.
Enlarge the point (4, 3) by scale factor 2, centre (1, 1).

footings.skill: List equally likely outcomes and count each once
footings.teach: List every outcome so each one is equally likely. A coin and a spinner numbered 1 to 3 give H1, H2, H3, T1, T2 and T3, six outcomes. When order does not matter, a pair like AB is the same as BA, so count it once.

probes.prompt: Two fair coins are flipped. What is the probability of one head and one tail?
Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 3?
How many different pairs can you choose from 4 people, if order does not matter?

footings.skill: Use the right total for a probability
footings.teach: The total is the group you are picking from at that moment. If 1 of 10 sweets is eaten, the next pick is out of 9. If you are told the person wears glasses, the total is only the people who wear glasses.

probes.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue counters. A red counter is taken out and not put back. What is the probability that the next counter is red?
In a club of 20, 12 play football and 3 of those also play chess. A football player is picked at random. What is the probability that they play chess?
In a class of 30, 15 wear glasses and 10 are left-handed. 5 are left-handed and wear glasses. A student who wears glasses is picked. What is the probability they are left-handed?

footings.skill: Find class width, frequency density and quartiles
footings.teach: Class width is the upper boundary take away the lower one, and frequency density is frequency ÷ class width: 10 ≤ x < 40 has width 30, so frequency 60 gives density 2. The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower quartile, not the largest value minus the smallest.

probes.prompt: The class 20 ≤ t < 35 has frequency 45. Find its frequency density.
A histogram bar for 0 ≤ x < 5 has frequency density 4. How many values are in that class?
Find the interquartile range of 1, 3, 8, 9, 12, 20, 24.

footings.skill: Add and subtract column vectors
footings.teach: Add or subtract the top numbers, then the bottom numbers: (2, 5) − (3, 1) = (−1, 4). To go from P to Q, go back to O and then out again, so PQ = −p + q.

probes.prompt: Work out the column vector (3, 2) + (1, −4).
Work out the column vector (5, 1) − (2, 3).
OA = a and OB = b. Write the vector AB in terms of a and b.

footings.skill: Find and use the nth term of a sequence
footings.teach: Sequences start at n = 1, so test a rule by putting n = 1 and n = 2 back in: for 2, 7, 12, … the rule 5n − 3 gives 2, then 7. Counting from 3 to 6 including both ends gives 4 numbers, not 3.

probes.prompt: Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, …
The nth term of a sequence is 4n − 1. Find the 10th term.
How many whole numbers are there from 5 to 12, counting both 5 and 12?

footings.skill: Check you answered what was asked
footings.teach: Before you write the answer, reread the last line of the question. If a = 5 and it asks for 3a − 2, then 5 is only a step and 13 is the answer.

probes.prompt: A shirt costs £20. It is reduced by 15%. What is the new price?
3x = 12. Find the value of 2x + 1.
A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm and length 9 cm. Find its area.

concepts.name: Negative number
concepts.oneSentence: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign in front.
concepts.picture: The night temperature in Shimla is 2 °C. It drops by 5 degrees. It passes zero and lands on −3 °C. On a number line, negative numbers sit to the left of 0.
steps: To add a negative number, move left. 4 + (−6) = −2.
To subtract a negative number, move right. 4 − (−6) = 10.
To multiply or divide, work out the size first. Then count the minus signs.
An even count of minus signs gives a positive answer. An odd count gives a negative answer.
concepts.workedExample: Work out (−6) × 5. The size is 6 × 5 = 30. There is one minus sign, so the answer is negative. (−6) × 5 = −30.

check.prompt: Work out (−8) ÷ (−2).

mixUp.name: the take-away sign
mixUp.how: In 7 − 3 the sign is an instruction to take away. In −3 it is part of the number.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Factor
concepts.oneSentence: A number that divides exactly into another number, with nothing left over.
concepts.picture: 24 students can line up in 4 equal rows of 6. So 4 and 6 are both factors of 24. They cannot make 5 equal rows, so 5 is not a factor of 24.
steps: Try dividing by 1, 2, 3 and so on.
Each time it divides exactly, write down the pair. For 24: 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6.
Stop when the pairs start to repeat. The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24.
concepts.workedExample: Find the factors of 18. The pairs are 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6. 4 and 5 do not divide exactly. The next pair would be 6 × 3, which repeats. So the factors are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.

check.prompt: How many factors does 12 have?

mixUp.how: The factors of 12 are 12 or smaller. The multiples of 12 are 12 or bigger.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Multiple
concepts.oneSentence: What you get when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3 and so on.
concepts.picture: A bus leaves every 6 minutes. It leaves at 6, 12, 18 and 24 minutes past the hour. Those times are the multiples of 6.
steps: Write the number.
Keep adding the same number: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30.
That list is its times table, and it never ends.
concepts.workedExample: Is 42 a multiple of 6? 6 × 7 = 42, so yes. Is 44? 44 ÷ 6 leaves 2 over, so no.

check.prompt: What is the 5th multiple of 7?

mixUp.how: Multiples of 6 are 6 or bigger: 6, 12, 18. Factors of 6 are 6 or smaller: 1, 2, 3, 6.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Power
concepts.oneSentence: A short way to write a number multiplied by itself several times.
concepts.picture: You forward a message to 3 people. Each of them forwards it to 3 more. In the 4th round it reaches 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 people. We write that as 3⁴.
steps: The big number is the base. It is the number being multiplied.
The small raised number is the index. It says how many times the base appears.
Write it out and multiply. 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.
concepts.workedExample: Work out 5³. The base is 5 and it appears 3 times. 5 × 5 × 5 = 25 × 5 = 125.

check.prompt: Work out 2⁴.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Fraction
concepts.oneSentence: A number that says how many equal parts of a whole you have.
concepts.picture: Cut a roti into 4 equal pieces and eat 3. You have eaten 3/4 of the roti. The 4 says how many pieces make the whole. The 3 says how many you took.
steps: The bottom number says how many equal parts make one whole.
The top number says how many of those parts you have.
A fraction is also a division. 3/4 means 3 ÷ 4, which is 0.75.
When the top equals the bottom, you have exactly 1 whole. 4/4 = 1.
concepts.workedExample: What fraction of an hour is 20 minutes? An hour has 60 minutes, so it is 20/60. Divide the top and the bottom by 20. It is 1/3 of an hour.

check.prompt: A bar of chocolate has 8 equal squares. You eat 3. What fraction is left?

mixUp.name: two separate numbers
mixUp.how: 3/4 is one number, a little less than 1. It is not a 3 and a 4 sitting side by side.

concepts.name: Decimal place
concepts.oneSentence: A position for a digit to the right of the decimal point.
concepts.picture: A price of ₹12.75 has two digits after the point. The 7 is in the first decimal place and stands for 7 tenths. The 5 is in the second and stands for 5 hundredths.
steps: The first place after the point is tenths. The second is hundredths. The third is thousandths.
To count decimal places, count the digits after the point. 3.142 has three.
To round to 2 decimal places, keep two digits after the point and look at the third.
If that third digit is 5 or more, round the last kept digit up.
concepts.workedExample: Round 3.14159 to 2 decimal places. Keep 3.14 and look at the next digit, which is 1. It is less than 5, so the answer is 3.14.

check.prompt: Round 7.286 to 2 decimal places.

mixUp.how: Decimal places are counted from the decimal point. Significant figures are counted from the first digit that is not zero.

concepts.name: Area
concepts.oneSentence: The amount of flat space a shape covers, counted in unit squares.
concepts.picture: A classroom floor is laid with square tiles, 8 along and 5 across. It holds 8 × 5 = 40 tiles, so its area is 40 tiles.
steps: Pick a unit square, such as 1 cm by 1 cm.
For a rectangle, count the squares in one row: that is the length.
Count the rows: that is the width.
Multiply, so the area is length × width, in square units such as cm².
concepts.workedExample: A table top is 12 cm by 9 cm. Its area is 12 × 9 = 108 cm². Cut it into a 12 by 5 piece and a 12 by 4 piece, and the areas 60 and 48 still make 108.

check.prompt: A rug is 7 m long and 3 m wide. What is its area in m²?

mixUp.name: the perimeter
mixUp.how: The perimeter is the distance round the edge. The 7 m by 3 m rug has area 21 m² but perimeter 20 m.

concepts.name: Percentage
concepts.oneSentence: A number out of 100, written with the sign %.
concepts.picture: A test has 100 marks and you score 73. That is 73%. A phone showing 40% battery has 40 parts left out of every 100.
steps: Per cent means out of 100. So 25% is 25/100, which is 1/4 or 0.25.
To find 10% of an amount, divide it by 10. 10% of ₹350 is ₹35.
Build other amounts from 10% and 1%. 30% is three lots of 10%, and 5% is half of 10%.
To write a fraction as a percentage, make its bottom number 100. 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%.

check.prompt: What is 20% of 250?

mixUp.name: the amount itself
mixUp.how: 20% is not 20. It is 20 out of every 100, so 20% of 50 is 10 and 20% of 500 is 100.

concepts.name: Angle
concepts.oneSentence: The amount of turn between two lines that meet, measured in degrees.
concepts.picture: A door swinging open from its frame. A quarter of the way round, it makes a right angle, 90°. Half a turn is 180°, a straight line, and a full turn is 360°.
steps: Put the centre of the protractor on the corner where the two lines meet.
Line up 0° with one of the lines.
Read the scale where the other line crosses it, counting up from that 0°.
concepts.workedExample: A straight line is half a turn, 180°. So a 130° angle on a straight line leaves 180° − 130° = 50° beside it.

check.prompt: A clock's hands point at 12 and at 3. What angle do they make?

mixUp.name: the length of the lines
mixUp.how: Drawing the lines of an angle longer does not make it bigger. The angle is the turn between them, not how far they reach.

concepts.name: Set
concepts.oneSentence: A collection of things with a clear rule for what is in it.
concepts.picture: The days of the week that start with S make a set: {Saturday, Sunday}. Ask of any day whether it starts with S, and the answer is yes or no.
steps: Write the members inside curly brackets, with commas between them.
Write each member once. {1, 1, 2} is the same set as {1, 2}.
Order does not matter. {1, 2} and {2, 1} are the same set.
A set with nothing in it is the empty set, written { }.
concepts.workedExample: Write the vowels in the word CRICKET as a set. Check each letter: C no, R no, I yes, C no, K no, E yes, T no. The set is {I, E}, with 2 members.

check.prompt: How many members does the set of letters in the word APPLE have?

mixUp.name: a list
mixUp.how: A list can repeat things, and its order matters. A set holds each thing once, in any order.

concepts.name: Member
concepts.oneSentence: One of the things inside a set.
concepts.picture: Asha sings in the school choir, so she is a member of the set of choir singers. You do not sing in the choir, so you are not a member.
steps: Read the rule of the set.
Test the thing against the rule.
If it passes, write ∈, as in 4 ∈ {2, 4, 6}. If it fails, write ∉, as in 5 ∉ {2, 4, 6}.
concepts.workedExample: Is 15 a member of the multiples of 5? 15 = 3 × 5, so yes. Is 22? 22 ÷ 5 leaves 2 over, so no.

check.prompt: A = {2, 3, 5, 7}. How many of the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 are members of A?

mixUp.how: A member is one thing: 2 ∈ {1, 2, 3}. A subset is a set: {2} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}. The curly brackets tell you which.

concepts.name: Universal set
concepts.oneSentence: Everything you are choosing from in one problem, drawn as the box around a Venn diagram.
concepts.picture: When you sort the 30 students in your class into teams, the universal set is all 30 students. A student from another school is not in it.
steps: Decide what the problem is about: students, numbers or letters.
Write that whole collection as ξ.
Every other set in the problem must fit inside ξ.
Anything in ξ but outside every circle still counts.
concepts.workedExample: ξ is the whole numbers from 1 to 10, and A is the even numbers in ξ. Then A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}. 12 is even, but it is not in ξ, so it is not in A.

check.prompt: ξ is the whole numbers from 1 to 12. A is the multiples of 4 in ξ. How many members does A have?

mixUp.how: The union is everything inside the circles. The universal set is the whole box, including what lies outside every circle.

concepts.name: Venn diagram
concepts.oneSentence: A picture of sets as circles inside a box, where an overlap shows what the sets share.
concepts.picture: Draw a box for your class of 30. Draw one circle for cricket and one for football. Students who play both go where the circles overlap.
steps: Draw a box for the universal set.
Draw one circle for each set, overlapping.
Fill in the middle first: the things in both.
Then fill in the rest of each circle, and last of all the outside.
concepts.workedExample: In a class of 30, 12 play chess, 10 play carrom and 4 play both. Put 4 in the middle. Chess only is 12 − 4 = 8. Carrom only is 10 − 4 = 6. Outside is 30 − 8 − 4 − 6 = 12.

check.prompt: In a Venn diagram, 9 things are in A, 6 are in B and 2 are in both. How many are in A only?

mixUp.name: two separate circles
mixUp.how: Draw the circles apart only when nothing is in both. If even one thing is shared, they must overlap.

concepts.name: Intersection
concepts.oneSentence: The things that are in both sets at once.
concepts.picture: The friends who like mango are {Asha, Bilal, Chetan}. The friends who like guava are {Bilal, Divya}. Only Bilal likes both, so the intersection is {Bilal}.
steps: Go through the members of the first set.
Keep each one that is also in the second set.
Write what you kept. If you kept nothing, the intersection is the empty set.
concepts.workedExample: A = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9} and B = {3, 6, 9}. 3 is in both, and so is 9. Nothing else is. So A ∩ B = {3, 9}.

check.prompt: A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} and B = {5, 10, 15}. How many members does A ∩ B have?

mixUp.how: ∩ means in both, so it is never bigger than either set. ∪ means in either, so it is never smaller.

concepts.name: Union
concepts.oneSentence: Everything that is in one set or the other or both, with each thing written once.
concepts.picture: The mango fans are {Asha, Bilal, Chetan} and the guava fans are {Bilal, Divya}. Everyone who likes either fruit is {Asha, Bilal, Chetan, Divya}. Bilal is written once.
steps: Write every member of the first set.
Add each member of the second set that is not already there.
To count it without listing, use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
concepts.workedExample: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4, 5}. Start with 1, 2 and 3. Add 4 and 5, because 2 and 3 are already there. A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, with 5 members. Check with the rule: 3 + 4 − 2 = 5.

check.prompt: A has 8 members, B has 5, and 3 are in both. How many members does A ∪ B have?

mixUp.how: ∪ looks like the letter U, for union: everything in either set. ∩ is the same shape upside down: only what is in both.

concepts.name: Complement
concepts.oneSentence: Everything in the universal set that is not in a given set.
concepts.picture: In a class of 30, 18 play cricket. The other 12 do not. Those 12 are the complement of the cricket players.
steps: Find the universal set, ξ.
Take away every member of A.
What is left is A′. Its count is n(ξ) − n(A).

check.prompt: ξ has 25 members and A has 9. How many members does A′ have?

mixUp.name: the opposite
mixUp.how: The complement depends on ξ. If ξ is 1 to 10, the complement of the even numbers is {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}. Change ξ and A′ changes too.

concepts.name: Subset
concepts.oneSentence: A set whose members are all inside another set.
concepts.picture: Every girl in your cricket team is in the cricket team. So the girls in the team make a subset of the team.
steps: Take each member of the smaller set.
Check that it is also in the bigger set.
If every one passes, it is a subset. One failure and it is not.
The empty set and the whole set always count as subsets.
concepts.workedExample: Is {2, 4} a subset of {1, 2, 3, 4}? 2 is in it and 4 is in it, so yes: {2, 4} ⊆ {1, 2, 3, 4}. Is {2, 5}? 5 is not in it, so no.

check.prompt: How many of these are subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4}: {1, 4}, {2, 5}, { } and {3}?

mixUp.how: A member is one thing: 3 ∈ {1, 2, 3}. A subset is a set: {3} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}.

concepts.name: Power set
concepts.oneSentence: The set of every subset of a set, including the empty set and the whole set.
concepts.picture: A chaat stall can add sev, curd and chutney. Each possible plate, from no topping to all three, is one subset. All 8 plates together make the power set.
steps: Take the members one at a time.
Each member is either in a subset or out of it: 2 choices.
Multiply the choices. 3 members give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 subsets.
A set with n members has 2ⁿ subsets.
concepts.workedExample: How many subsets does {red, green, blue, yellow} have? Each colour is in or out. That is 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, which is 2⁴.

check.prompt: A set has 5 members. How many members does its power set have?

mixUp.how: A subset is one choice, like {sev}. The power set is the set of all the choices together.

concepts.name: If-then statement
concepts.oneSentence: A claim that whenever one thing is true, a second thing is true as well.
concepts.picture: If it is Sunday, then the school is closed. Every Sunday tests the promise. One Sunday with the school open would make the claim false.
steps: Split the claim into its if part, p, and its then part, q.
Look for a case where p is true.
Check whether q is true there too.
One case with p true and q false shows the claim is false.
concepts.workedExample: Test: if a number is a multiple of 6, then it is even. 6, 12 and 18 are even. And 6 = 2 × 3, so every multiple of 6 is 2 × something. The claim is true.

check.prompt: Claim: if a number is a multiple of 4, then it is a multiple of 8. What is the smallest whole number above 0 that breaks it?

mixUp.name: the claim turned round
mixUp.how: Swapping the parts makes a new claim. If it is Sunday, the school is closed. But a closed school does not mean it is Sunday. It could be a holiday.

concepts.name: Counterexample
concepts.oneSentence: One case that shows an if-then claim is false: the if part holds and the then part does not.
concepts.picture: Someone says every bird can fly. A penguin is a bird that cannot fly. One penguin is enough to show the claim is false.
steps: Write the claim as: if p, then q.
Look for something that makes p true.
Among those, look for one that makes q false.
If you find one, the claim is false. Show it and stop.
concepts.workedExample: Claim: if two numbers are odd, their sum is odd. Try 3 and 5. Both are odd, and 3 + 5 = 8, which is even. So 3 and 5 are a counterexample, and the claim is false.

check.prompt: Claim: every number in the 4 times table is also in the 6 times table. What is the smallest counterexample above 0?

mixUp.name: an example that fits
mixUp.how: Examples that fit a claim never prove it. Only a reason does. A counterexample works the other way: one is enough to disprove it.

concepts.name: Contrapositive
concepts.oneSentence: The if-then statement you get by swapping the two parts and putting not in front of each.
concepts.picture: If it is Sunday, then the school is closed. Its contrapositive is: if the school is open, it is not Sunday. Both say the same thing.
steps: Write the statement as: if p, then q.
Swap the parts: if q, then p.
Put not in front of each part: if not q, then not p.
This is true exactly when the first statement is true.
concepts.workedExample: Find the contrapositive of: if a shape is a square, then it has four sides. Swap and add not: if a shape does not have four sides, then it is not a square. A triangle has three sides, and it is not a square.

check.prompt: Statement: if a number is a multiple of 10, then it ends in 0. A number ends in 7. Is it a multiple of 10? Answer yes or no.

mixUp.name: swapping without the nots
mixUp.how: Swapping alone gives if q, then p, which can be false when the statement is true. The contrapositive swaps and adds not to both parts, and it always agrees.

concepts.name: Truth table
concepts.oneSentence: A table with one row for every way the parts of a claim can be true or false.
concepts.picture: To check a claim about A and B, ask two questions of each member: in A? in B? There are only four mixes of answers: yes yes, yes no, no yes, no no. Four rows cover everyone.
steps: List the parts: in A? in B?
Write one row for each mix of yes and no. Two parts give 4 rows.
Work out the claim on each row.
Two claims mean the same thing if they agree on every row.
concepts.workedExample: Check that "not in A or B" matches "not in A and not in B". Row yes, yes: both say no. Row yes, no: both say no. Row no, yes: both say no. Row no, no: both say yes. They agree on all four rows.

check.prompt: A claim has three parts, and each can be true or false. How many rows does its truth table need?

mixUp.how: A Venn diagram shows the four kinds of member as four regions. A truth table lists the same four kinds as rows.

concepts.name: De Morgan's laws
concepts.oneSentence: Two rules for the complement of a union or an intersection: the dash moves inside, and ∪ and ∩ swap.
concepts.picture: The students who play neither cricket nor football are the ones who miss cricket and also miss football. Not in cricket-or-football is the same as not in cricket and not in football.
steps: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′. Outside either circle means outside both.
(A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. Outside the middle means outside at least one circle.
When the dash moves inside the brackets, swap ∪ and ∩.

check.prompt: ξ has 30 members and 7 of them are in A ∩ B. How many members does A′ ∪ B′ have?

mixUp.name: moving the dash without swapping
mixUp.how: (A ∪ B)′ is not A′ ∪ B′. In a class of 30 with 7 in both, A′ ∪ B′ has 23 students, while only 4 might play neither.

concepts.name: Prime number
concepts.oneSentence: A whole number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself.
concepts.picture: 7 students can only line up as 1 row of 7 or 7 rows of 1. No other equal rows work, so 7 is prime. 6 students can make 2 rows of 3, so 6 is not.
steps: Try dividing by 2, 3, 5, 7 and so on.
If nothing divides exactly before the pairs repeat, the number is prime.
Remember that 1 is not prime. It has only one factor.
The first few primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19.
concepts.workedExample: Is 29 prime? It is odd, so 2 does not divide it. 29 ÷ 3 leaves 2 over. 29 ÷ 5 leaves 4 over. 6 × 6 is already more than 29, so there is nothing bigger to check. 29 is prime.

check.prompt: Which of these is prime: 21, 23 or 27?

mixUp.name: odd numbers
mixUp.how: 9, 15 and 21 are odd but not prime. And 2 is prime but not odd.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Prime factors
concepts.oneSentence: The prime numbers that multiply together to make a number.
concepts.picture: Think of primes as bricks that cannot be split. 12 is built from the bricks 2, 2 and 3, because 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. No other set of prime bricks makes 12.
steps: Split the number into any two factors. 60 = 6 × 10.
Split each part again until every part is prime. 6 = 2 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5.
Write the primes in order. 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
Check by multiplying back. 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60.
concepts.workedExample: Write 84 as a product of primes. 84 = 2 × 42. 42 = 2 × 21. 21 = 3 × 7. So 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. Starting with 84 = 7 × 12 gives the same four primes.

check.prompt: Write 30 as a product of prime factors.

mixUp.how: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Its prime factors are only 2, 2 and 3.

usedIn.label: Chapter 1 · Negative numbers, primes and powers

concepts.name: Highest common factor
concepts.oneSentence: The biggest number that divides exactly into both numbers.
concepts.picture: You have 12 samosas and 18 jalebis. You want identical plates with nothing left over. The most plates you can make is 6, each with 2 samosas and 3 jalebis. So the HCF of 12 and 18 is 6.
steps: List the factors of each number. 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
Find the ones in both lists: 1, 2, 3 and 6.
Take the biggest: 6.
